Dozens of metal NPs, and especially AgNPs, have been used in antimicrobial therapy for chronic wounds.163 However, metal deposition can cause DNA and cell damage. Hence, nanomaterials that prevent infection without causing toxicity are required. Further effort should be made to decrease the accumulation of heavy metals. Alternatively, nanocomposites without metal elements should be adopted more often in the future. To overcome the ever-changing environment of the skin during chronic wound healing, several wound-monitoring and stimuli-responsive biomaterials have been developed.58,157,218 By leveraging specific characteristics, such as the photothermal effect, chemo-dynamic effect, fluorescence, and thermo-sensitivity, more nano-biomaterials that can be used in stimuli-responsive and dynamic monitoring systems for wound care should be developed. Most studies on wound healing have focused on migration-promoting effects, antimicrobial activity, and substance delivery. However, few nanotech-based multifunctional smart systems, such as smart dressings that show specific responses to stimuli, have been developed. Researchers in this field should work towards developing smart systems based on the mechanisms of disunion in chronic wounds, which could effectively demonstrate the potential of nanobiotechnology in promoting chronic wound repair. Despite the decades-long history of nanotechnology research, few products and therapies based on nanobiotechnology have become available commercially or entered the clinical trial phase. One reason for this is that most basic nanotech research on chronic wound healing is performed in rodent models, such as C57BL/6 mice or Sprague–Dawley rats, even though the skin structure and chronic wound healing processes differ between rodents and humans.222 The wound healing effects observed in primates, such as humans, may not be as good as those in rats and mice. Meanwhile, the cost of nano-materials and processing platforms required for large-scale preparation also hinder the clinical translation of nanotechnologies. During the past few years, numerous nano-materials and techniques have been used to repair chronic wounds. This review summarizes some nanobiotechnology-based systems and nanoplatform designs that can be used for treating chronic wounds. It highlights that a smart dressing for chronic wounds that allows real-time monitoring and has stimuli-responsive abilities is one possible direction for the future of nano-wound-repairing systems. We hope this review motivates the development of more sophisticated wound management systems based on nanobiotechnology in the future.

title: Poloxamer-based hydrogel with EGCG and rhEGF for diabetic foot ulcer treatment
abstract: A thermosensitive hydrogel dressing was developed for the healing of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) using Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) and recombinant human epidermal growth factor (rhEGF). Hyaluronic acid (HA), poloxamer 407 (P407), and pectin (PE) were used to form the sol-gel transition matrix, which exhibited a sol-to-gel transition around 30 °C. The hydrogel was physiologically stable. Structural and morphological characterization using Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) confirmed the efficient incorporation of EGCG and rhEGF in a porous nanoarchitecture. Rheological analysis showed the storage modulus is quite constant over the frequency range (0.01–10 Hz), and compression analysis showed a compressive strength of 40.85 kPa, ensuring mechanical appropriateness for various wound conditions. This hydrogel had a water content of 76.64% and a water vapor transmission rate of 6011.44 g/m2/day, favorable to maintain a moist wound surface. Antibacterial tests showed inhibition rates of 73.53% against Escherichia coli and 75.37% against Staphylococcus aureus. In vitro with RAW 264.7 macrophages and L929 fibroblasts showed >90% cell survival, increased migration with 92.53% wound closure by 48 h, strong antioxidant activity, and considerable decrease in TNF-α and IL-6 (pro-inflammatory cytokines). Combining a natural antioxidant and bioactive protein within a responsive hydrogel matrix presented a synergistic solution, holding significant promise for enhancing diabetic wound healing by antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and regenerative processes. The fabrication of the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel, an advanced wound dressing designed for diabetic foot ulcers

sections.text: DFUs have long been characterized as one of the most severe and expensive diabetes mellitus complications, the result of a multifactorial relationship between peripheral neuropathy, vascular insufficiency, and impaired immune defense. Neuropathy reduced pain sensitivity, rendering the patient susceptible to unrecognized trauma, while impaired peripheral circulation and chronic hyperglycemia compromised tissue healing and increased susceptibility to infection. All of these factors came together to ensure prolonged wound persistence, typically resulting in gangrene or amputation if not addressed, thus the demanding need for advanced therapeutic interventions to enhance healing and prevent unfavorable outcomes [1–4]. Hydrogel dressings for wounds were a novel method of DFU management because of their ability to form a moist environment, promote proliferation of cells, and induce angiogenesis. Their three-dimensional polymeric hydrophilic networks also enabled controlled delivery of therapeutic agents like antimicrobial agents, antioxidants, and growth factors [5–10]. The traditional hydrogel formulations were not multifunctional and hence their use in treating the multifunctional pathophysiology of diabetic wounds, like oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and cell dysfunction, was compromised. To address these limitations, a new composite hydrogel system was constructed using HA, P407, and PE. Each of these was chosen for its contribution to wound healing. HA, an essential component of the extracellular matrix, facilitated re-epithelialization by promoting keratinocytes and fibroblasts, angiogenesis, and inflammation control [11–14]. P407, a thermosensitive triblock copolymer, exhibited a sol-to-gel transition at near physiological temperature, providing an easy target for topical application and in situ drug delivery [15–19]. PE, a plant polysaccharide, exhibited high biocompatibility and bioadhesiveness, providing structural strength and further facilitating controlled release of the incorporated therapeutics [20–25]. Incorporation of EGCG and rhEGF in the hydrogel matrix introduced multifunctional bioactivity. EGCG, a potent green tea catechin, has previously demonstrated antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial activities. It served to reduce oxidative stress, enhance fibroblast migration, and induce angiogenesis in diabetic ulcers [26–30]. rhEGF played a pivotal role in stimulating cellular proliferation and differentiation, thereby accelerating re-epithelialization and collagen synthesis, processes impaired in diabetic wound healing [31–36]. While previous work examined single-component or two-agent hydrogels, none of them have combined this specific set of HA, P407, PE, EGCG, and rhEGF in one thermoresponsive system for diabetic wound healing [37–41]. The formulation treated multiple pathological characteristics simultaneously, such as oxidative imbalance, chronic inflammation, and impaired tissue regeneration. This study aimed to synthesize and investigate the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel as a bioactive composite dressing for DFUs. The hydrogel was evaluated for its physicochemical properties, biocompatibility, capacity to heal fibroblast migration, tissue repair, and regeneration. Its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities were also assessed using in vitro diabetic wound models. Generally, the aim was to formulate this hydrogel as a stable and multi-functional platform for improved tissue repair and complication prevention in DFUs. The fabrication of the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel, an advanced wound dressing designed for DFUs, is illustrated in Graphical Abstract 1.

Poloxamer 407 (P407, ≥99% purity), Hyaluronic Acid (HA, sodium salt, Mw ~1.5 MDa, ≥95% purity), and Pectin (PE, derived from apple, ≥98% purity) were obtained from Thermo Fisher Scientific. Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG, ≥95% purity), 1-Ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl) carbodiimide hydrochloride (EDC, ≥98% purity), N-Hydroxysuccinimide (NHS, ≥98% purity), and Hydrogen Peroxide (H₂O₂, 30% w/w, analytical grade) were also procured from Thermo Fisher Scientific. Phosphate Buffered Saline (PBS, pH 7.4), deionized water (resistivity >18 MΩ cm), Lysozyme solution (≥40,000 units/mg protein), Luria–Bertani (LB) medium, Chloramphenicol (purity ≥98%), Dimethyl Sulfoxide (DMSO, ≥99.9%), Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NADH, disodium salt, purity ≥98%), Nitro Blue Tetrazolium Chloride (NBT, ≥98%), Phenazine Methosulfate (PMS, ≥98%), and antioxidant enzyme test kits were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich, USA. Recombinant human Epidermal Growth Factor (rhEGF, ≥98% by SDS-PAGE) was purchased from PeproTech, R&D Systems. RAW 264.7 macrophage cells, L929 mouse fibroblast cells, Escherichia coli (ATCC 25922), and Staphylococcus aureus (ATCC 25923) were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, USA).

25 wt% Poloxamer 407 was dissolved in cold deionized water (4 °C) and stirred overnight. 2 wt% HA and 2 wt% pectin were dissolved separately in deionized water and stirred until fully dissolved. The HA, PE, and P407 solutions were combined and stirred at 4 °C to avoid gelation. After that, EGCG was dissolved in PBS and added to the polymer mixture at 0.2 wt%. Meanwhile, 10 μg/mL rhEGF stock solution was added to the mixture and stirred gently. Crosslinking agent EDC/NHS was added, and pH was adjusted to 7.4. The mixture was poured into molds and gelled by warming to room temperature (~30 °C). After gelation, the hydrogels were thoroughly washed with PBS (pH 7.4) to eliminate loosely bound EDC/NHS residues. Then, the samples were dialyzed against deionized water by using dialysis tubing with an MWCO of 12–14 kDa for 48 h at 4 °C, while the dialysis water was changed every 6 h. UV-Vis spectroscopy was used to assess residual EDC/NHS removal efficiency. This method created a bioactive hydrogel for wound healing with EGCG and rhEGF.

We analyzed HA, P407, PE, HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels using FT-IR spectroscopy (Shimadzu IR affinity-1S). The examined samples were frozen before testing to maintain their structural integrity and avoid moisture interference in the measurement. The samples’ transmission infrared spectra were obtained after subtracting the background spectra. The wavelengths were collected between 4000 cm−1 and 500 cm−1 with a resolution of 4 cm−1. The crystal structures of rhEGF and EGCG-loaded hydrogels were studied using an X-ray diffractometer (JDX-3532 JEOL Japan). Data were captured at a speed rate of 2◦/min, scanning voltage of 45 kV, and scanning current of 40 mA. We converted the collected data into a diffraction program using Origin software (Origin Lab, MA, USA) and evaluated the data. SEM (Hitachi, S4800, Tokyo, Japan) was used at 20 kV (voltage) to study the microstructure of HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels. The thawed samples were treated with gold sputter coating before observation to increase the conductive properties of the hydrogels. HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels were dispersed in water, dropped on a carbon grid, and air-dried. TEM from JEOLJEM-2100 was used at 200 kV to study the shape and size of the hydrogels, and the images were captured.

A rheometer was used at room temperature (25 °C) for all dynamic rheological measurements. The measuring procedures were followed. The samples underwent an amplitude sweep to determine their linear viscoelastic characteristics. The process included enclosing the testing samples between the parallel plates, regulating the shear frequency (10 Hz), and exposing the samples to a strain of 0% to 1000%. This allowed for determining the frequency-dependent changes in the modulus of storage G’, modulus of loss G”, and the viscosity η of the samples in response to strain. After determining the range of longitudinal strain, sweeps in frequencies were performed in a constant strain condition (0.01–10 Hz) to provide graphs exhibiting the G’ and G” fluctuations. Each sample underwent triplicate measurement of rheological properties.

Shanghai Pour Technology Instrument Co., LTD’s QJ210 universal testing equipment, which has a 500 N load cell, was used to test hydrogel compression. The ASTM D695-15 standard was followed for mechanical testing. The hydrogel samples were molded into the shape of a cylinder measuring 15 mm in diameter and 10 mm in height. The compression study was performed at a rate of 50 mm/min to calculate the hydrogel’s modulus of compression and the compression stress at which point the hydrogel sample was cracked or 80% damaged, devoid of cracking was noted. The hydrogel’s compression modulus was then determined using the formula and shown as a stress-strain graph. where, F = the stress at which the hydrogel sample cracks or 80% damage. Shydrogel = the hydrogel sample’s area of stress.

The hydrogels’ strength of adhesiveness was determined using a conventional approach, including tensile load testing, to determine tissue adhesives. Tissue adhesion was determined using fresh pig skin. Pig skins were cut into slices of rectangular shape that measured 2 mm in thickness, 20 mm in length, and 15 mm in width. The rectangular slices were immersed for 24 h in a solution of NaCl before being kept in PBS for further use. PBS-moistened pig skin slices received 500 μL of HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE precursor solutions without hydrogel formation. After 10 min of contact between the two pig skin slices, the pre-treated slices were clamped in the middle of the testing equipment. QJ210 testing equipment from Shanghai Pour Technology Instrument Company, which featured a 100 N load cell and operated at 5 mm/min, was used to measure the strength of adhesiveness. At the separating point, the strength of adhesiveness was measured. Five samples were included in each batch of hydrogels, and each sample’s measurements were recorded five times.

At 37 °C, the cylinder-shaped hydrogel samples were completely immersed in PBS solution (0.01 M). Every two hours, the hydrogel samples were taken apart, the leftover solution of PBS was carefully wiped from the outermost layer, and they were checked for weight until their weight had not changed further. The SR of the hydrogel samples was calculated using the formula. where, Wt = the initial weight of the hydrogel sample. Ws = the weight of the swelled hydrogel sample. Five repetitions of each experiment were conducted.

After soaking for 24 h, the hydrogel was taken out from the PBS solution using the same procedure as for SR measurement. After carefully removing the remaining water from the surface, the weight of the freeze-dried hydrogel sample was determined to be W0. The hydrogel sample’s EWC was calculated using the formula. where, Ws = the initial weight of the hydrogel sample. W0 = the weight of the freeze-dried hydrogel sample. Five repetitions of each experiment were conducted.

The 30 mL glass vials were filled with more than 90% water. The positive control group consisted of glass vials with no lids, while the HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE groups consisted of vials with hydrogel coverings. After applying the hydrogel to the vial apertures, the weight was noted as Wi. Following an incubation period of 24 h at 37 °C, the vials were taken out, weighed, and noted as Wt. The transmission of gas from the hydrogel sample was measured by calculating the weight variation before and following the incubation period for 24 h. A cylinder-shaped mold was prepared from the hydrogel sample, measuring 1 cm in thickness and diameter. Where, Wi = the initial weight of the hydrogel sample and water-filled vial. Wt = the weight of the hydrogel sample and the vial after water evaporation for 24 h. A = the vial aperture area in m2. t = time in days. Five repetitions of each experiment were conducted.

The GF of the HA, HA-P407, and HA-P407-PE hydrogel systems was measured to assess crosslinking efficiency and structural stability at physiological conditions. Dry hydrogel samples were weighed initially (W0) and subsequently submerged in PBS, pH 7.0, at 37 °C. At set time points (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 24, and 48 h), the samples were taken out, blotted lightly with cellulose filter paper to remove surface moisture, and reweighed to determine the swollen mass (Wf). Subsequently, the hydrogels were dried in a hot-air oven at 40 ± 2 °C for 24 h or to constant weight, ensuring complete removal of the solvent. The constant weight after drying was utilized to compute the gel fraction through the following equation: Each formulation was evaluated with 21 samples (n = 21), including seven replicates from three independent synthesis batches. A similar procedure was conducted with simulated body fluid (SBF), formulated to mimic physiological ionic conditions, to further assess the structural integrity of the hydrogels in biomimetic conditions [42].

sections.section: Studies on drug release in vitro
sections.text: To calculate the EGCG and rhEGF release, the prepared 2 g of EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE was placed in a pH 8.5 10 mL PBS buffer-filled centrifuge tube. Stir the centrifuge tube in a water bath shaker at 37 °C. The released medium was taken out for examination at certain intervals and refilled with an equivalent volume of the new medium to maintain consistency. We used a UV-visible spectrophotometer to measure the release of rhEGF and EGCG. OD595 nm values were noted. The cumulative drug release of rhEGF and EGCG was calculated using the formula. Where, Qn = the cumulative drug release rate (%) at the nth time point. Cn = the drug concentration (mg/mL) in the nth specimen. V = the total volume (mL) of the release medium. Vi = the volume (mL) of the sample withdrawn at the ith time point. W0 = the initial weight (mg) of the hydrogel sample with rhEGF and EGCG.

The biological degradation of hydrogel samples in vitro was evaluated with 2 × 104 U/mL of lysozyme in PBS. The hydrogel sample was molded into a cylinder shape with 3 cm in height and 1 cm in diameter and then placed in a solution of lysozyme. A 37 °C incubator was used to incubate the hydrogel samples, and every 24 h, the lysozyme solution was replaced. The weight of the deteriorating hydrogel sample was frequently evaluated. Where, W0 = the hydrogel’s initial weight. Wt = the hydrogel’s weight at degradation time t. The results are noted with three simultaneous measurements for each sample. The mean ± SD is used to represent the findings.

sections.section: Assessment of antibacterial effectiveness in vitro
sections.text: The liquid bacteriostatic technique was employed to determine the antibacterial properties of HA, HA-P407, and HA-P407-PE hydrogels. Bacterial suspensions were prepared by incubating individual E. coli and S. aureus colonies at 37 °C in an LB medium for the whole night. A dilution of 4 × 108 CFU/mL was done with the suspension of bacterial cells. To prepare hydrogel extracts, 2 g of hydrogel was UV sterilized, washed with sterile pH 7.4 PBS, immersed in 10 mL of LB liquid medium, and then incubated for 24 h at 37 °C. A 0.22 μm filter membrane was sterilized to filter these extracts. 4 mL of the extract was mixed with 40 μL of the diluted bacterial solution. The blank control group received equal amounts of distilled water, LB medium, and 0.5 mg/ml chloramphenicol. Hydrogel extract and LB medium were given to the test group, whereas LB medium was given to the positive control group. For 12 h, samples in each group were kept at 37 °C at 180 rpm/min in an incubator, and the OD values were determined at 600 nm. The below formula is used to evaluate the resistance of antimicrobial bacteria. OD0 = the typical growth value of the standard bacterial solution OD1 = the sample’s background value OD2 = the test group’s bacterial solution’s typical growth value

sections.section: Assay for in vitro antioxidant capability
sections.text: The antioxidative properties of HA, HA-P407, and HA-P407-PE hydrogels were evaluated using the reported procedure [43]. A test tube was filled with 0.4 g of the hydrogel mixture and 4 mL of the ABTS+ working solution. The OD 734 nm was measured after 1 h of incubation in the dark at room temperature. Triplicate experiments were carried out for every sample. The following formula was used to calculate the samples’ rate of scavenging against radicals of ABTS+. where, A0 = the absorbance of the ABTS+ working solution at the beginning Ai = the absorbance of the ABTS+ working solution combined with the hydrogel sample at various intervals DPPH was evaluated by combining 4 mL of the DPPH working solution with 0.4 g of the hydrogel mixture in each test tube. After one hour of incubation at room temperature in dark conditions, the resulting mixture’s OD517 nm was noted. Triplicate experiments were carried out for every sample. The below formula was used to calculate the samples’ rate of scavenging against the radicals of DPPH. where, A0 = the DPPH free radical solution’s absorbance before the sample addition Ai = the DPPH free radical solution’s absorbance after combining with the hydrogel sample at various periods The following procedure was used to test the scavenging of superoxide anion (O2−) radicals. The PBS solution containing 1 mL of 936 mmol/L NADH, 300 mmol/L NBT, and 120 mmol/L PMS was added to the testing samples, with groups devoid of hydrogel as control. After vortexing, the mixture was allowed to settle at room temperature for half an hour in the dark. The OD570 nm was noted, and the scavenging rate of superoxide anion was calculated using the formula below. where, A0 = the OD570 nm of the control group Ai = the OD570 nm of the hydrogel group

To check the hydrogels’ protective impact against intracellular oxidative stress, we tested the viability of RAW 264.7 cells grown with H2O2 following treatment with hydrogel. A 96-well plate was used to culture the cells with 1 × 104 cell density in each well. After 12 h of culturing, a new growth medium containing an equal amount of H2O2 and hydrogel was added to the cells. As a positive control, cells were grown in 0.5 mmol/L H2O2 and DMEM equivalent to the hydrogel extract volume. The medium was withdrawn after culturing for 4 h, then MTT was used, and the viability of cells was determined. The absorbance readings for the test, control, and blank groups are Ahydrogel, Acontrol, and Ablank. Superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT) are two common antioxidant enzymes that RAW 264.7 cells produce in response to oxidative stress. These enzymes help fight intracellular stress due to oxidation and keep metabolic processes normal [44]. Therefore, to assess how hydrogels affect cellular antioxidant activity, this study analyzed the antioxidant responses of RAW 264.7 cells using SOD and CAT test kits. We used the manufacturer-recommended formulas to do the estimations.

Hydrogel extracts were tested for in vitro cytotoxicity using the MTT assay on L929 cells. Fetal bovine serum, penicillin-streptomycin (10 KU/mL–10 mg/mL), and DMEM high-glucose medium were combined in a volume ratio of 100:10:1 to form a complete medium. The hydrogels were immersed in the complete medium for 24 h (0.1 g of hydrogel in 1 mL of complete medium) to prepare hydrogel extracts. After that, the mixture was sterilized and impurities were removed using a sterile syringe. 96-well plates were cultured with L929 cells (1 × 104 cells/well) and 200 μL of complete media to achieve the best possible cell adherence. The plates were then incubated for 24 h with 5% CO₂ at 37 °C. The investigation included five groups: untreated control, H2O2, HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel treatments (Hydrogel treatment groups- L929 cells following incubation with the specific hydrogel-containing solution (20 µM of HA-P407-PE/ rhEGF@HA-P407-PE/ EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE) and H2O2). After substituting 200 μL of hydrogel extract for the original medium, they are left to incubate for 24, 48, and 72 h. The samples were incubated for 4 h after 100 μL of a complete medium solution containing MTT (5 mg/mL) was added to the hydrogel extract again. The formazan crystals were broken down by removing the top layer of the medium and then adding 150 μL of DMSO while stirring. The OD490 nm was noted. Cells in the control group were cultured with the complete medium, while those in the test group were given a solution of hydrogel extract. The formula was used to determine the cellular viability. For the test, control, and blank groups, the absorbance readings are Ahydrogel, Acontrol, and Ablank.

sections.section: Staining with acridine orange (AO) and ethidium bromide (EB)
sections.text: Apoptosis was evaluated qualitatively in vitro using AO and EB staining. The L929 cells were cultured in 24-well plates at a density of 2 × 104 cells/mL. The investigation included five groups (control, H2O2, HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel treatments) with 24 wells for each group. The cells were treated with trypsin (20 μL/well) and washed with PBS following a 24-h culture. One hundred microliters of suspension of cells was mixed with 4 μL of a dual fluorescent staining solution containing 100 μg/mL of AO and EB, respectively. We transferred the stained solutions to glass slides, allowing for subsequent examination under a fluorescence microscope (Olympus BX-51, Japan). This approach allows for the visual differentiation of live cells from dead ones by analyzing their fluorescence.

A total of 1 × 104 L929 cells were added to each well of a 96-well plate. Each group received different treatment conditions. The investigation included five groups: untreated control, H2O2, HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel treatments, which were incubated at 37 °C for 72 h. The control comprised untreated cells. Following the instructions provided by SAB, USA, we used the Cell Counting Kit-8 test to evaluate the proliferation of cells. OD450 nm was noted. To compare cell proliferation, acridine orange (AO) staining was used.

The levels of ROS inside the cells were detected with a commercial ROS Assay Kit. L929 cells were grown in 6-well plates (5 × 105 cells/mL), and the investigation included five groups: untreated control, H2O2, HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel treatments. The cells were exposed to 10 μM of Dichloro-dihydro-fluorescein diacetate (DCFH-DA) at 37 °C for 30 min in the absence of light. A fluorescent microscope was used to visualize ROS generation after three washes with serum-free DMEM.

The migration of the cells was evaluated in a wound-healing study that employed the wound scratch technique. The investigation included five groups: untreated control, H2O2, HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel treatments. L929 cells were grown on six-well plates and treated with HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels for 24 h. After recombining them with suspension, every six-well plate was reseeded with 2 × 104 cells. Sterile 1 mL micropipette tips were used to damage the cells once they reached monolayer growth. To eliminate the remaining substance, we washed the cells with PBS. Images were taken immediately following the damage and again after different incubation periods (6, 12, 24, and 48 h). The gap distance was measured using the software ImageJ (National Institutes of Health).

sections.section: Analysis of mRNA expression by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR)
sections.text: Following the supplier’s guidelines, cells were lysed and total RNA was extracted using TRIzolTM reagent. Utilizing 4× Super RT Mix (100 mM), the RNA underwent reverse transcription to produce cDNA. The amounts of mRNA expressed were determined using qRT-PCR detection equipment (Bio-Rad Real-Time PCR Detection System, USA). qRT-PCR analysis was performed using the 2−ΔΔCt method to assess relative gene expression. GAPDH served as the internal control for normalization. Fold changes were determined by normalizing target gene Ct values to GAPDH (ΔCt), followed by comparison with the control group (ΔΔCt). Supplementary data Table 1 shows the list of primers.

The data was analyzed using students’ t-test or one-way ANOVA, with P-values less than 0.05 indicating statistical significance. Statistical findings are presented graphically as mean ± SD. Where *** indicates P < 0.001, ** indicates P < 0.01, * indicates P < 0.05, and NS indicates P > 0.05.

The EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel was successfully prepared with a transparent and homogeneous appearance and no sign of phase separation. When warmed to around 30 °C, the formulation formed a sol-gel transition to give a stable, self-sustaining hydrogel network. After gelation, extensive washing and a 48-hour dialysis process effectively removed residual EDC/NHS, as determined by UV-Vis spectroscopy, which indicated minimal absorbance related to the crosslinking agents, as shown in Supplementary Fig. S1.

The characterization of the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel was conducted using FT-IR, XRD, SEM, and TEM analyses. The FT-IR spectra of HA, P407, PE, HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels are illustrated in Fig. 1A. FT-IR spectra confirmed the successful integration of EGCG and rhEGF within the HA-P407-PE hydrogel matrix. The O-H stretching band of HA appeared around 3300 cm−1, while the C-H stretching of P407 was observed near 2900 cm−1. Bands corresponding to carboxyl and ester groups of PE were detected around 1700 cm−1 and 1200 cm−1, indicating effective interactions among HA, P407, and PE [45]. Additionally, bands at 1600 cm−1 and 1650 cm−1 confirmed the presence of EGCG and rhEGF, consistent with prior studies on biopolymer integration [46]. XRD patterns of HA, P407, PE, HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels are illustrated in Fig. 1B. XRD analysis revealed structural changes in the HA-P407-PE hydrogel upon the addition of EGCG and rhEGF. Pure HA exhibited broad bands indicative of semi-crystallinity, while P407 and PE displayed sharp crystalline bands. The band intensity decreased after incorporating EGCG and rhEGF, suggesting a shift toward a more amorphous structure. SEM images of HA-P407-PE hydrogel are illustrated in Fig. 2A, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel are illustrated in Fig. 2B. SEM imaging demonstrated that the addition of EGCG and rhEGF enhanced the hydrogel’s porous network. The HA-P407-PE hydrogel exhibited uniform, interconnected pores, which are advantageous for cellular infiltration and nutrient exchange during wound healing. TEM images of EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel are illustrated in Fig. 2C. TEM analysis revealed well-dispersed nanostructures within the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel, with uniform nanoscale particle size.

The rheological performance of the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel was evaluated through strain and frequency sweeps. The rheological performance of the hydrogels is illustrated in Fig. 3A. Strain sweeps demonstrated that the hydrogel maintained structural integrity across a strain range of 0–1000%, with the storage modulus (G’) greater than the loss modulus (G”), indicating predominant elastic behavior. This property is critical for stability during application to wound sites. Frequency sweeps conducted under constant strain conditions (0.01–10 Hz) revealed that both G’ and G” remained stable, demonstrating excellent shear-thinning properties.

Compression test strain-stress graphs of hydrogels are illustrated in Fig. 3B. Compression testing revealed that the hydrogel exhibited a robust compressive modulus, indicating its ability to withstand mechanical forces, which is essential for maintaining structural integrity in wound healing applications. The compressive modulus was derived from strain-stress graphs.

Adhesion testing was performed using tensile load testing on fresh porcine skin. The adhesion strength of the hydrogels is illustrated in Fig. 3C. The EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel demonstrated significantly higher adhesion strength compared to other formulations, highlighting its potential for effective tissue integration in wound healing. This enhanced adhesion may be attributed to the synergistic effects of EGCG and rhEGF, promoting better interaction at the tissue interface. P < 0.001 for HA-P407-PE and P < 0.01 for HA-P407 compared to HA.

The SR of the hydrogels is illustrated in Fig. 3D. The SR of the hydrogel was assessed, revealing significant swelling due to the hydrophilic nature of its components. This property is essential for wound healing as it enhances moisture retention and absorption of exudates. The results align with previous studies showing that similar hydrogels effectively retain water and promote a moist healing environment, facilitating cellular activities and controlled release of therapeutic agents.

The EWC of the hydrogels is illustrated in Fig. 3E. The EWC of the hydrogel was evaluated, demonstrating high water retention capacity. This property is critical for promoting cellular activities and enhancing therapeutic agent diffusion, particularly in diabetic wounds. High EWC supports the hydrogel’s mechanical properties, enabling it to retain structure while providing necessary moisture for tissue regeneration. P < 0.001 for HA-P407-PE and HA-P407 compared to HA.

The WVTR of the hydrogels is illustrated in Fig. 3F. The WVTR of the hydrogel was assessed to determine its ability to maintain a moist wound environment. Results showed significant WVTR, indicating effective moisture transmission while minimizing fluid loss. Maintaining optimal moisture is crucial for improving cell migration and reducing infection risk in wound repair. P < 0.001 for HA-P407-PE and HA-P407 compared to HA.

The GF% of the hydrogels in PBS and SBF is illustrated in Supplementary Figs S2 and S3, respectively. The GF of HA, HA-P407, and HA-P407-PE hydrogels was assessed in PBS and SBF for 48 h. In PBS, the lowest GF was exhibited by HA (49.12%), followed by HA-P407 (64.72%), whereas the highest GF was exhibited by HA-P407-PE (79.24%) at 24 h. In SBF, slightly lower GF values were detected: 47.20% for HA, 62.25% for HA-P407, and 75.55% for HA-P407-PE at 24 h. Statistical analysis supported significant differences between formulations.

sections.section: Studies on drug release in vitro
sections.text: The in vitro drug release profiles of EGCG and rhEGF from the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel were evaluated to assess its potential for sustained therapeutic delivery. The cumulative release percentages of rhEGF and EGCG over time are illustrated in Fig. 4A. The results demonstrated a biphasic release pattern, characterized by an initial burst release followed by a gradual and sustained release phase.

The in vitro degradation profile of the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel was evaluated for 7 days, as illustrated in Fig. 4B. The results demonstrated a gradual decrease in the residual weight of the hydrogel, indicating effective and controlled degradation over time.

sections.section: Assessment of antibacterial effectiveness in vitro
sections.text: The antibacterial properties of HA, HA-P407, and HA-P407-PE hydrogels were evaluated against E. coli and S. aureus, two common pathogens associated with wound infections. The decline in bacterial growth is illustrated in Fig. 4C. The results demonstrated that HA-P407 and HA-P407-PE hydrogels exhibited significant antibacterial activity, with the HA-P407-PE hydrogel showing the highest inhibition rates against both E. coli and S. aureus.
The antioxidant capacities of HA, HA-P407, and HA-P407-PE hydrogels were evaluated using ABTS, DPPH, and superoxide anion scavenging assays.

The absorbance of the mixture of ABTS⁺ and hydrogel was measured, and the scavenging rate was calculated. The results, illustrated in Fig. 4D, showed that HA-P407-PE exhibited the highest antioxidant potential among the tested hydrogels. P < 0.001 for HA-P407-PE and HA-P407 compared to HA.

The absorbance was measured, and the scavenging rate was calculated similarly. As illustrated in Fig. 4E, HA-P407-PE demonstrated superior DPPH radical inhibition compared to HA and HA-P407. P < 0.001 for HA-P407-PE and HA-P407 compared to HA.

The absorbance was measured, and the scavenging rate was calculated. The results, illustrated in Fig. 4F, indicated significant scavenging activity in all hydrogels, with HA-P407-PE showing the most pronounced effects. P < 0.001 for HA-P407-PE and HA-P407 compared to HA. The HA-P407-PE hydrogel exhibited the highest antioxidant activity across all assays.

The intracellular antioxidant ability of the hydrogels was evaluated using RAW 264.7 cells incubated in a solution containing hydrogel and H2O2. Phase contrast images, illustrated in Fig. 5A, showed that cells treated with the hydrogels maintained higher viability compared to the control group. Quantification of cell viability, as illustrated in Fig. 5B, confirmed that hydrogel treatment significantly enhanced cell survival in the presence of H2O2-induced oxidative stress. The quantification of superoxide dismutase (SOD) metabolism, illustrated in Fig. 5C, and catalase (CAT) metabolism, illustrated in Fig. 5D, revealed elevated enzyme activities in hydrogel-treated cells. In all the above analyses, P < 0.001 for HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE compared to the H2O2 group.

The in vitro cytotoxicity of the hydrogels was evaluated using L929 cells incubated in a solution containing hydrogel extracts. Phase contrast images are illustrated in Fig. 6A, showing that cells treated with HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels maintained higher viability compared to the control group. Quantification of cell viability, as illustrated in Fig. 6B, confirmed that these hydrogel groups exhibited significantly higher cell viability after 3 days of incubation. P < 0.001 for HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE compared to the H2O2 group. These results suggest that HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels possess favorable biocompatibility.

Apoptosis in L929 cells was qualitatively assessed using acridine orange (AO) and ethidium bromide (EB) staining. Fluorescent images are illustrated in Fig. 7A, showed that live cells, which took up AO, exhibited green fluorescence, while dead cells, which allowed EB penetration, displayed strong orange fluorescence [47]. The quantification of apoptosis is illustrated in Fig. 7B, revealed that treatments with HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels significantly reduced cell death compared to the H₂O₂-treated control group. P < 0.001 for HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE compared to the H2O2 group.

Cell proliferation was assessed using the CCK-8 assay, with optical density (OD) values measured to quantify cell viability and proliferation. Fluorescent images using AO staining, illustrated in Fig. 8A show that L929 cells treated with HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels exhibited enhanced proliferation compared to the H₂O₂-treated control group. The quantification of cell proliferation is illustrated in Fig. 8B, confirming that these hydrogel treatments significantly increased cell proliferation compared to the H₂O₂ group. The H₂O₂ group showed reduced cell viability, highlighting the protective and proliferative effects of the hydrogels. P < 0.001 for HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE compared to the H2O2 group.

The generation of ROS in L929 cells was quantified using the DCFH-DA method. Fluorescence images, depicted in Fig. 9A, showed that the H₂O₂-treated group exhibited significantly elevated ROS levels compared to the untreated control, confirming the induction of oxidative stress by hydrogen peroxide. In contrast, treatment with HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels significantly reduced ROS generation compared to the H₂O₂ group. The quantification of ROS levels, illustrated in Fig. 9B, confirmed these findings, demonstrating the hydrogels’ ability to mitigate oxidative stress in L929 cells. P < 0.001 for HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE compared to the H2O2 group.

Cell migration was assessed using a wound-healing assay in L929 cells. Fluorescent images of scratch assays after 48 h of incubation in a solution containing hydrogel and H₂O₂ are shown in Fig. 10A. The quantification of wound area closure, illustrated in Fig. 10B, revealed that the untreated control and H₂O₂-treated groups exhibited minimal cell migration into the wound area, reflecting impaired healing due to oxidative stress. In contrast, treatment with HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels significantly enhanced cell migration compared to the H₂O₂ group. Among these, the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel demonstrated the highest migratory potential. P < 0.001 for HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE compared to the H2O2 group.

The mRNA expression levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and iNOS) were evaluated using qRT-PCR, with GAPDH serving as an internal control. The results, illustrated in Fig. 11, demonstrated that treatment with HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels significantly reduced the expression of these pro-inflammatory markers compared to the H₂O₂-treated control group. Among the hydrogel formulations, EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE exhibited the most pronounced downregulation of IL-1β, IL-6, iNOS, and TNF-α mRNA levels. For all the mRNA expression levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines evaluated, P < 0.001 for HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE compared to the H2O2 group. These findings suggest that the hydrogels, particularly EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, possess potent anti-inflammatory properties.

Successful synthesis of the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel shows that natural and synthetic polymers could be integrated with bioactive molecules by a mild, biocompatible procedure. Cold processing at 4 °C and the temperature-sensitive sol-gel transition were utilized to ensure structural and functional integrity of thermolabile materials such as rhEGF. P407 was primarily responsible for facilitating thermoreversible gelation, whereas HA and PE were responsible for biocompatibility and the viscoelasticity of the hydrogel. The application of EDC/NHS chemistry ensured mild crosslinking conditions without the requirement for aggressive initiators or UV, especially useful in wound healing applications. EGCG, which is rich in antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities, and rhEGF, a strong mitogenic factor for epithelial cells, were incorporated into the hydrogel matrix successfully. The lack of turbidity or precipitation indicated good compatibility and potential interactions among EGCG, rhEGF, and the polymer matrix [48–52]. Effective removal of EDC/NHS, as determined by UV-Vis spectroscopy, highlights the necessity of post-gelation purification to minimize possible cytotoxicity of carbodiimide chemistry. Dialysis against a 12–14 kDa MWCO tubing for 48 h with frequent water changes ensured the removal of free crosslinkers, thus improving the safety profile of the hydrogel for biomedical use. This fabrication process produces a bioactive, structurally stable, and biocompatible hydrogel for wound healing with the further therapeutic benefit of EGCG and rhEGF [53, 54]. A schematic representation of hydrogel fabrication showing antioxidant, antibacterial, and anti-inflammatory properties and improving cell viability, proliferation, and migration is illustrated in Scheme 1. The characterization of the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel highlights its innovative formulation as a bioactive wound-healing matrix. The FT-IR spectroscopy validated the successful crosslinking and integration of the components into the hydrogel matrix. The presence of protein-specific amide bands and EGCG-related peaks suggests the successful physical and potentially covalent entrapment of the bioactive agents. These spectral bands are in line with EDC/NHS-mediated conjugation and validate that the hydrogel is an appropriate drug and protein delivery vehicle. XRD characterization favored the assumption that the rhEGF and EGCG were encapsulated in an amorphous state, which is desirable for increased bioavailability and controlled release. Amorphous EGCG in the hydrogel can ensure its gradual diffusion and therapeutic efficacy while healing in wound sites [55]. SEM analysis gave information on the surface morphology and internal structure of the hydrogels. Interconnected porosity is advantageous for gas and nutrient exchange in wound environments. Porosity and surface texture changes upon EGCG loading indicate increased polymer interactions, which can be responsible for enhanced mechanical strength and sustained release behavior [56]. TEM imaging also confirmed the formation of nanoscale hydrogel domains. The spherical and irregular morphologies reflect self-assembly during gelation, and the comparatively uniform size distribution suggests a stable network. The nanoscale dimensions and morphology are also desirable for deep tissue penetration and cellular uptake, which are important in wound healing applications [57]. These findings validate that EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel exhibits highly integrated structural, morphological, and compositional properties that can be the right option to produce effective wound healing therapy. Rheological characterization generated key information regarding the viscoelasticity and mechanical stability of the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel. The detection of a wide linear viscoelastic zone through amplitude sweep measurement indicates that the hydrogel can support physiological strains without prompt breakdown, qualifying it for topical and in situ delivery in DFU. The prevalence of storage modulus (G’) over loss modulus (G”) across the range of frequencies signifies a gel-like response characterized by elastic recovery, which is important to sustain hydrogel shape, offer structural strength, and achieve good contact with the wound surface. The higher G’ values in the EGCG-rhEGF-loaded formulation signify strengthened polymeric interactions, most probably through hydrogen bonding and potential covalent crosslinking through EDC/NHS chemistry. The shear-thinning nature is another positive attribute since it enables the hydrogel to be shearable under shear stress (e.g., injection or spreading), but restores its structure once the stress is eliminated. Such a property further increases its usefulness in clinical applications, especially for irregular or deep wounds. The higher viscosity and mechanical strength of EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel further indicate a denser network, likely a result of the physical and chemical interactions among EGCG, rhEGF, and the polymer matrix. These characteristics are a direct outcome of enhanced retention, controlled release performance, and enhanced wound healing efficiency. The rheological characteristics justify the stability, mechanical integrity, and application potential of the hydrogel as a bioactive and responsive wound dressing [58]. This property is particularly important for wound healing applications, where the hydrogel must withstand mechanical forces while facilitating controlled drug release [59, 60]. Mechanical characterization of the hydrogels indicated that the addition of EGCG and rhEGF greatly improved the mechanical strength and compressive modulus of the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel relative to other formulations. The higher breakage resistance and compressive modulus are expected to result from increased intermolecular interactions, such as hydrogen bonding and electrostatic forces between EGCG, rhEGF, and the polymer network. The occurrence of EDC/NHS-mediated crosslinking could have helped to create a denser and more stable hydrogel network. These interactions lead to enhanced load-bearing ability and deformation resistance under compressive loads. Such mechanical stability is crucial in ensuring the integrity of the hydrogel during application on dynamic wound surfaces, leading to sustained adhesion and functionality. Therefore, the enhanced mechanical properties of the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel make it a good option for application as a durable and bioactive wound dressing [61]. This aligns with previous studies highlighting the importance of mechanical strength in hydrogels for load-bearing applications, such as tissue regeneration in chronic wounds [62]. Adhesive strength analysis showed that the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel possessed higher tissue adhesion compared to the other types of formulations. Improved adhesiveness is due to the multifunctional attributes of EGCG, which contain catechol groups that can mimic the mussel foot protein adhesive moieties and result in more enhanced tissue surface interactions. In addition, the presence of rhEGF could have contributed to enhanced interfacial bonding due to its proteinaceous nature, which improves hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions with the tissue matrix. Hydrophilic polymers HA, P407, and PE created a good gel environment that enabled close contact and spreading onto the tissue surface, which is critical in effective adhesion. The enhanced adhesivity of EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel comes with significant benefits for wound healing applications, where tight bonding to moist wound surfaces must be achieved to ensure efficient localized drug delivery and shielding against external pathogens [63]. This property is critical for ensuring the hydrogel’s stability and retention at the wound site, facilitating sustained release of therapeutic agents [64]. The swelling response of hydrogels is a key parameter that influences their drug release kinetics, biocompatibility, and capacity to create a moist wound environment. The resultant increase in swelling rate in the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel indicates that the incorporation of EGCG and rhEGF improves the hydrophilicity and the water-retaining capacity of the hydrogel. EGCG has several hydroxyl functional groups that lead to more hydrogen bonding with water molecules, resulting in greater fluid intake. rhEGF as a protein further contributes to the hydrophilic character of the matrix. The HA-P407-PE base hydrogel already has good swelling characteristics because of the water solubility of its constituents, but introducing bioactive agents further enhances this property. An increase in swelling without loss of structure shows a stable network of the hydrogel capable of holding wound exudate without loss of structural integrity, which is advantageous for wound healing applications [65]. EWC is a crucial parameter indicating the hydrogel’s capacity to retain hydration, an essential parameter for cellular activity support and wound healing. The EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel had the highest EWC, indicating improved water-holding capacity. This is due to the synergistic action of hydrophilic ingredients HA, P407, and PE, along with EGCG and rhEGF, both of which contain functional groups (hydroxyl and amino acids, respectively) that absorb and hold water. The enhanced EWC leads to a hydrated wound environment, which is crucial for epithelialization and granulation tissue development. The mechanical strength of the hydrogel was retained even at high water content, as a clear indication of strong network formation and suitability for long-term biomedical applications like wound dressing [66]. These properties align with previous studies showing that hydrogels with high water retention capacity are more effective in facilitating wound healing, particularly in DFU, where moisture regulation is critical [67–70]. WVTR analysis also indicates the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel’s efficacy in achieving a perfect moisture balance, important for wound healing. A perfect WVTR enables adequate gaseous exchange with protection from wound desiccation or excessive fluid retention, which is very important in maintaining cell migration, reducing the risk of infection, and facilitating tissue regeneration. The EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel had a lower WVTR than other hydrogel groups, reflecting better moisture retention. This improved property can be attributed to the constricted polymeric network and high intermolecular hydrogen bonding promoted by the addition of EGCG and rhEGF, which collectively suppress water permeability. The measured WVTR is within the optimal range needed for efficient wound repair, conducive to a moist healing environment, and low bacterial penetration. These results highlight the hydrogel’s value as a next-generation wound dressing that can induce rapid and efficient tissue regeneration [71]. Compared to predicate works, the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel offers a unique combination of rheological, mechanical, and adhesive properties, along with high water retention and moisture transmission capabilities [72]. GF analysis shows HA-P407-PE hydrogels to be higher in crosslinking and structural stability than HA and HA-P407. Low GF of pure HA hydrogels suggests weak crosslinking and solubility, which weaken mechanical strength and durability. The addition of P407 enhanced network stability by thermoresponsive micellization, showing improved crosslinking than that of HA. The HA-P407-PE system showed the highest GF due to extra hydrogen bonding and ionic interactions that were introduced by PE, leading to a denser and more stable hydrogel matrix. The increased GF has a direct relationship with enhanced mechanical properties, swelling reduction, and stability under physiological conditions, which are essential parameters for biomedical applications like wound healing. Slightly decreased GF values in SBF than in PBS indicate that ionic interactions in physiological-like conditions can slightly affect polymer stability. The HA-P407-PE hydrogels preserved considerably better structural integrity even in SBF, further supporting their potential for in vivo applications. The improved stability of HA-P407-PE hydrogels guarantees the integrity of the material upon long-term exposure to body fluids, enabling sustained mechanical performance and controlled therapeutic release. This is beneficial for wound healing applications, where the integrity of the hydrogel must be preserved for extended therapeutic efficacy. The GF analysis highlights the long-term biomedical application potential of HA-P407-PE hydrogels as a stable platform for sustained release of bioactive agents like EGCG and rhEGF [73]. While previous studies have explored individual aspects of hydrogel performance, this study integrates multiple properties into a single formulation, providing a comprehensive approach to wound healing [74]. The release profile of the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel shows its novel potential for controlled and sustained therapeutic delivery, which is vital for successful wound healing. The hydrogel displayed a biphasic release pattern, which had an initial burst followed by a sustained, prolonged release phase. The early burst offers quick delivery of EGCG and rhEGF to the wound site, meeting early therapeutic requirements such as reduction of oxidative stress, modulation of inflammation, and activation of tissue regeneration. Later, the sustained release phase provides ongoing delivery of therapeutic agents, aiding long-term processes such as re-epithelialization, collagen synthesis, and tissue remodeling. The controlled release properties are due to the stable entrapment of EGCG and rhEGF in the temperature-sensitive, porous HA-P407-PE gel matrix. Thermosensitive gelation at body temperature further modulates drug permeation, thus improving the suitability of the hydrogel for wound healing applications under physiological conditions in vivo. Slower release rates for rhEGF relative to EGCG might be due to its larger size or greater interactions with the hydrogel matrix, suggesting selective modification of release profiles according to molecular properties. In contrast to previous studies targeting the delivery of a single therapeutic molecule, the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel provides a synergistic strategy through the co-delivery of an antioxidant (EGCG) and a growth factor (rhEGF) from a single source. This dual function is especially beneficial for the treatment of chronic conditions such as DFU, where several biological processes need to be targeted simultaneously. The results of this research are in agreement with earlier studies that have highlighted the advantages of biphasic release systems in promoting wound healing efficacy. Conventional wound dressings tend to lack sustained delivery, while hydrogels with controlled release profiles, such as the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, provide therapeutic concentrations of bioactive agents for prolonged periods, enhancing healing efficiency. The EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel is a potential option for clinical translation, providing an efficient platform for sustained, controlled delivery of therapeutic agents, which is essential for effective management of chronic and complex wounds [75]. The degradation profile of EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel delineates its meticulously designed structure for long-term therapeutic delivery in wound healing. The hydrogel degraded gradually over 7 days under in vitro conditions. Such controlled degradation response is vital, so that the hydrogel offers sustained structural support yet facilitates the continuous release of the bioactive agents needed to control oxidative stress, regulate inflammation, and stimulate tissue regeneration. The hydrogel structure, more specifically the HA-P407-PE matrix and EDC/NHS-mediated crosslinking, is critical to maintaining mechanical stability and degradability in balance. This balance is necessary to coordinate the breakdown of the hydrogel with the wound healing schedule, avoiding premature degradation that might weaken the therapeutic effect, as well as prolongation, potentially inhibiting tissue integration or inducing foreign body responses. The EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel showed a slightly lower degradation rate than other formulations. This may be due to the higher crosslinking density or the interaction between the encapsulated EGCG and rhEGF with the polymer network, which can restrict lysozyme accessibility and increase the structural stability of the hydrogel. Such slower, controlled degradation is beneficial for chronic wound treatment, providing a sustained release of therapeutic agents over a long duration. In comparison to predicate studies, the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel exhibits a more precisely controlled degradation behavior, solving typical issues of either too fast or too slow degradation of hydrogels. Earlier hydrogels usually could not sustain optimal therapeutic concentrations over extended periods or cause unwanted tissue reactions. The EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel couples degradation and drug release with the nature of wound healing, thus facilitating efficient tissue regeneration. The findings stress the significance of controlled degradation for biomedical hydrogels. Gradual degradation in the presence of lysozyme under physiological conditions of the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel justifies its applications in clinical areas, particularly DFU treatment involving complex wounds with prolonged therapeutic intervention as a factor of successful cure [76]. The antibacterial efficacy of the HA-P407-PE hydrogel highlights its novel design for infection control, a significant aspect of wound healing, especially in chronic wounds such as DFU. The addition of P407 and PE in the hydrogel matrix greatly improved its antimicrobial activity against E. coli and S. aureus, showing it to be capable of creating a more conducive wound repair environment. The enhanced antibacterial property is owed to the synergy of contributions by the components of the hydrogel. P407, whose mode of action involves disrupting bacterial membranes, and PE, which probably prevents adhesion and proliferation of bacteria, collectively create a hydrogel that effectively inhibits infection while aiding in tissue regeneration. This multipronged approach possesses benefits compared to earlier approaches, where single antimicrobial agents like silver nanoparticles or antibiotics were used and proved to cause problems of resistance by bacteria or cytotoxicity. In comparison to previously reported hydrogels in the literature, HA-P407-PE presents a more sustainable and safer alternative by taking advantage of the intrinsic properties of its constituents instead of relying on external antimicrobial additives. The hydrogel exhibited significant antibacterial activity, although relatively lower than the positive control. The antibacterial activity of the hydrogel is extremely useful for wound healing purposes, where balanced antibacterial activity is necessary to suppress infection without disturbing beneficial microbiota that are vital for healing. HA-P407 hydrogels showed some antibacterial activity, though less significant than HA-P407-PE, indicating the significance of PE in improving the hydrogel’s antimicrobial property. The results indicate that additional functionalization, for example, by adding specific antibacterial agents or functional groups, may further enhance the hydrogel’s infection-prevention property without compromising its biocompatibility and mechanical stability [77]. E. coli (Gram-negative) and S. aureus (Gram-positive) were selected for their clinical relevance as common early colonizers and opportunistic pathogens in DFU. Representing two major bacterial classes, they enabled evaluation of broad-spectrum antibacterial activity. Although other pathogens like Pseudomonas aeruginosa and S. epidermidis are also implicated, E. coli and S. aureus are frequently isolated in early infection stages, supporting their use as representative strains for initial testing [78–80]. The HA-P407-PE hydrogel is an important breakthrough in the design of bioactive wound-healing materials, especially for diseases that are associated with heightened oxidative stress, like diabetic wounds. Oxidative stress, triggered by overproduction of ROS, is a significant barrier to successful wound healing. H₂O₂ was used to induce oxidative stress and mimic early-stage tissue damage and ROS-related cellular dysfunction typical of chronic wounds [81]. Its reproducibility and ability to create a controlled oxidative environment made it suitable for initial studies [82]. Although diabetic wounds also involve chronic inflammation driven by TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β, cytokine-based models such as LPS or IL-1β stimulation were recognized as more representative of prolonged inflammatory conditions and will be considered for future investigations [83, 84]. The antioxidant activity of the hydrogel, as evidenced by ABTS, DPPH, and superoxide anion scavenging assays, indicates its potential to establish a beneficial microenvironment for tissue regeneration through reducing oxidative damage. The improved antioxidant activity of the HA-P407-PE hydrogel can be credited to the synergistic action of its components. HA is recognized for its biocompatibility and ability to regenerate tissue, while P407 and PE augment the structural integrity and antioxidant activity of the hydrogel. These components create an extremely hydrophilic network that enhances the presence of hydroxyl groups capable of neutralizing free radicals. In comparison to other antioxidant-based hydrogel systems with agents such as vitamin E, curcumin, or plant extracts, the HA-P407-PE hydrogel offers a more stable, sustained, and intrinsic antioxidant function without depending entirely on external additives that tend to suffer from problems of instability and poor bioavailability. In addition to its extracellular antioxidant effects, the HA-P407-PE hydrogel demonstrated remarkable intracellular protection [85]. When exposed to H₂O₂-induced oxidative stress, RAW 264.7 cells treated with HA-P407-PE maintained higher viability compared to cells treated with HA or HA-P407 hydrogels. This enhanced cellular protection suggests that the hydrogel not only acts as a direct scavenger of ROS but also supports cellular defense mechanisms. Upregulation of essential antioxidant enzymes, SOD and CAT, also supports the hydrogel’s capacity to activate intrinsic cellular antioxidant responses. Increased activities of SOD and CAT in hydrogel-treated cells indicate an enhanced capability to detoxify superoxide radicals and H₂O₂, overcoming both acute and chronic oxidative challenges. This two-way mechanism, direct scavenging of ROS and induction of cellular antioxidant defenses, has an important therapeutic benefit, particularly in chronic wounds where sustained oxidative stress can impair healing. The HA-P407-PE hydrogel performed better than HA and HA-P407 formulations in all radical scavenging tests. The capacity to neutralize various species of radicals reflects a broad protective action, which is essential for biological systems where various ROS species are responsible for tissue damage. These results are consistent with earlier studies highlighting the advantages of antioxidant hydrogels in enhancing cell survival, suppressing inflammation, and speeding up wound healing. The HA-P407-PE hydrogel presents a multifunctional platform that combines structural support, long-term antioxidant activity, and cellular defense stimulation. Its enhanced performance compared to traditional antioxidant delivery methods makes it promising for therapeutic applications outside wound healing, including tissue regeneration and inflammation-related therapies [86]. The in vitro cytotoxicity test highlights the high biocompatibility of HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels, a major prerequisite for their use in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine. The uniformly high cell viability observed in all hydrogel-treated groups, even after extended exposure, attests to their low cytotoxicity and safe interaction with biological systems. The good biocompatibility of hydrogel is due to its well-designed composition consisting of HA, P407, and PE in a supportive and non-toxic matrix. Bioactive agents like rhEGF and EGCG are added, which enhance the therapeutic efficacy without affecting safety. rhEGF enhances cell growth and tissue repair, whereas EGCG adds antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, producing a tissue-repair-favorable microenvironment. In comparison to traditional hydrogels described in the literature, some of which have cytotoxicity-related challenges or are limited in bioactivity, the HA-P407-PE-based hydrogels are a considerable improvement. With both natural and synthetic elements combined, they balance mechanical stability, biocompatibility, and biofunctionality. In contrast to some synthetic polymer-based hydrogels that could cause cytotoxicity or non-therapeutic hydrogels, the HA-P407-PE hydrogel platform is multifunctional for effective regenerative outcomes. The groups treated with hydrogel had good and stable cell viability at 24, 48, and 72 h, indicating that the hydrogels had long-term biocompatibility. This is opposed to the group treated with H₂O₂, which decreased cell viability substantially, indicating the oxidative stress-mediated toxicity and reaffirming the protective role of the hydrogels. Such results are consistent with the general body of literature highlighting the significance of biocompatibility in hydrogel design for biomedical applications. Biocompatible hydrogels play pivotal roles in encouraging adhesion, growth, and differentiation of cells, which are vital to tissue regeneration success. The HA-P407-PE hydrogel is an extension of such examples in that not only does it accommodate cell survival, but also presents therapeutic agents with active augmentation of tissue repair. The findings reassert the effectiveness of HA-P407-PE, rhEGF@HA-P407-PE, and EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogels as non-toxic and competent systems for tissue engineering and wound healing [87]. L929 murine fibroblasts were used for initial screening due to their reproducibility, well-characterized responses in cytotoxicity and wound healing assays, and relevance for standardizing bioactivity, as recommended by ISO 10993 for medical material testing [88]. While appropriate for preliminary evaluation, future studies involving primary human dermal or diabetic fibroblasts will be considered essential for greater clinical relevance and will be planned for subsequent in vivo investigations [89, 90]. The results of AO/EB staining suggest strong support for the protective activity of HA-P407-PE-based hydrogels against oxidative stress-induced apoptosis in L929 cells. Treatment with H₂O₂ strongly enhanced apoptotic activity, as evidenced by the predominance of red and yellow-orange fluorescence, indicating oxidative damage and cell death. HA-P407-PE hydrogel treatment decreased apoptotic activity, with the majority of cells displaying green fluorescence, though a few still had yellow-orange staining. This indicates that although HA-P407-PE provides biocompatibility and partial protection, there may be some residual minor stress responses. The addition of rhEGF to the hydrogel matrix (rhEGF@HA-P407-PE) further increased cell survival and exhibited a superior apoptosis reduction to that of HA-P407-PE alone. The superior effect lies in rhEGF being capable of triggering cell proliferation as well as healing mechanisms. EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel exhibited the most significant protective effect with the highest ratio of viable (green-stained) cells and the least apoptotic fluorescence. The combined antioxidant effect of EGCG and the regenerative activity of rhEGF effectively neutralized ROS, reduced oxidative damage, and favored cell survival. Unlike typical hydrogels that commonly draw on single mechanisms, physical protection, or isolated antioxidant delivery, the HA-P407-PE-based hydrogels present a multifunctional platform. Besides providing a supportive matrix, they also release powerful bioactive agents to neutralize oxidative stress, in line with the modern call for sophisticated materials in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine. These results are in line with earlier reports of the effectiveness of antioxidant-enriched hydrogels, including those containing EGCG, curcumin, or cerium oxide nanoparticles, to decrease oxidative damage and enhance cell viability. The HA-P407-PE hydrogel takes this further by synergizing antioxidant protection with growth factor-induced regenerative support, presenting a complete solution for augmenting tissue repair under oxidative stress. The AO/EB staining results validate that the HA-P407-PE-based hydrogels, especially the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE formulation, are very effective in preventing cells from oxidative stress-induced apoptosis and are thus a good option for wound healing and tissue regeneration applications. The cell proliferation experiments prove the high ability of HA-P407-PE-based hydrogels to stimulate cellular growth and counteract oxidative stress-induced damage. H₂O₂ treatment significantly decreased L929 cell growth, as indicated by reduced OD450 values, representing oxidative stress and compromised viability. HA-P407-PE hydrogel treatment provided partial protection, modestly enhancing cell proliferation compared to the H₂O₂ group. This enhancement probably arises from the hydrogel’s matrix support, facilitating cell adhesion and survival. The hydrogel matrix composed of HA, P407, and PE provided a supportive and slightly immunomodulatory scaffold. HA suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines and promoted tissue repair via CD44 receptor interaction [91]. P407 reduced leukocyte adhesion and infiltration in inflamed tissues [92]. PE exhibited immunomodulatory effects by inhibiting macrophage-driven inflammation [93]. Although these components showed modest individual anti-inflammatory effects compared to the loaded EGCG and rhEGF, their combined action contributed to a biocompatible environment favorable for modulating inflammation. Adding rhEGF to the hydrogel (rhEGF@HA-P407-PE) enhanced proliferation further, as evidenced by increased OD450 values and a higher percentage of viable (green-fluorescent) cells, demonstrating rhEGF’s function in activating cellular repair and regeneration. The EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel showed the most significant impact, recovering cell proliferation to a level close to that of controls. The synergistic effect of the strong antioxidant activity of EGCG and the regeneration-promoting activity of rhEGF created a very beneficial microenvironment for cell growth, keeping cells away from oxidative damage and promoting proliferation more effectively than either constituent alone. EGCG, beyond its well-known antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, promoted fibroblast proliferation through activation of ERK1/2 and PI3K/Akt signaling pathways [94, 95]. It also regulated cyclin D1 and other cell cycle proteins, facilitating cell cycle progression [96]. In vitro studies further supported its role in enhancing dermal fibroblast migration and proliferation, especially under oxidative stress conditions [97, 98]. In contrast to traditional hydrogels that generally offer either structural support or single-agent delivery, the HA-P407-PE platform provides a multi-functional strategy that combines structural support with bioactive antioxidant and growth-stimulating effects. This approach is consistent with evolving demands in tissue engineering for materials that meet both the short-term and long-term demands of oxidative stress and compromised regeneration. Our results are in line with previous research using bioactive hydrogels incorporated with growth factors such as Epidermal Growth Factor (EGF), Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF), or Fibroblast Growth Factor (FGF), but the employment of dual functionalities, proliferative and antioxidant, is a significant development. The EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel is therefore an excellent option for wound healing and tissue regenerative processes, where the proliferation of cells is essential [99]. Quantification of ROS generation logically shows the potential of HA-P407-PE-based hydrogels to suppress oxidative stress, an indispensable factor for tissue repair and regeneration. H₂O₂ treatment significantly increased intracellular levels of ROS, confirming the model of oxidative injury. All the hydrogel-treated groups had decreased ROS content, with the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE formulation showing the most significant antioxidant effect. Although HA-P407-PE hydrogel alone reduced ROS accumulation moderately, with the indication of some intrinsic protective ability, rhEGF further increased cellular resistance. Indirect contributions to oxidative protection are believed to have come from the regenerative activity of rhEGF, promoting repair processes in cells. The greatest reduction was seen with the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel, and this attests to the synergistic interaction between EGCG’s direct ROS scavenging capacity and rhEGF’s regenerative signaling activity. This multi-action approach is a huge improvement compared to conventional hydrogels, which generally tackle oxidative stress using one mechanism only, i.e., barrier establishment or individual antioxidant release. In comparison with previous research involving antioxidants such as curcumin or cerium oxide nanoparticles, the current system combines antioxidant activity with growth factor provision within a unified matrix, presenting an enhanced, overall therapeutic modality. Since overproduction of ROS is the biggest obstacle against chronic wound healing, particularly for DFU, the highly effective oxidative stress relief capability of the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel makes it an excellent option to increase cell survival, induce tissue regeneration, and enhance healing performance [100]. Scratch assay-based wound-healing investigation gave insight into the migration capacity of L929 cells upon different hydrogel treatments. Cell migration is a vital process for wound closure and tissue regeneration, and the findings indicate that hydrogel composition plays a significant role in migratory behavior. In the control, L929 cells showed slow cell migration and less than complete closure of the wound, indicating physiological wound healing advancement without external signals. Oxidative stress evoked by H₂O₂ significantly inhibited the migration of cells, as witnessed by the extensive wound gap after 48 h. This coincides with published reports showing that oxidative stress interferes with cellular communication and integrity and thus inhibits migration and healing of tissues. Treatment with the HA-P407-PE hydrogel moderately enhanced cell migration relative to the H₂O₂ group, which implies that the hydrogel matrix itself provides some support to injured cells. Yet, full wound closure was not observed, which means that HA-P407-PE without bioactive components is not enough to maximize cell migration. Marked improvement was noted with treatment using rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel. The incorporation of rhEGF efficiently promoted wound closure, indicative of rhEGF’s capacity to induce cell proliferation, migration, and tissue regeneration. These results highlight the pivotal importance of growth factor delivery in facilitating effective wound healing. The strongest impact on cell migration was observed with the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel. This category showed near-total wound closure, indicating a synergistic interaction between EGCG and rhEGF. The strong antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities of EGCG potentially shielded cells from oxidative stress, while rhEGF increased their proliferative ability. Both of these bioactive factors formed a suitable microenvironment that supported quick cell migration and healing. The HA-P407-PE system improves on this method by combining growth factor delivery and antioxidant protection in one platform, providing a more complete solution for chronic wounds where compromised cell migration and ongoing oxidative stress are significant impediments to healing. The research highlights the high value of the EGCG-rhEGF@HA-P407-PE hydrogel as a sophisticated biomaterial for wound healing treatment. With its ability to effectively facilitate cell migration and inhibit oxidative damage, the multifunctional hydrogel is a novel approach to accelerate wound closure and enhance healing performance, especially in chronic and hard wound environments [101]. The qRT-PCR experiment showed that oxidative stress caused by H₂O₂ significantly enhanced the expression of inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and the gene related to oxidative stress, iNOS.
