title: Diverse nanocomposites as a potential dressing for diabetic wound healing
abstract: Wound healing is a programmed process of continuous events which is impaired in the case of diabetic patients. This impaired process of healing in diabetics leads to amputation, longer hospitalisation, immobilisation, low self-esteem, and mortality in some patients. This problem has paved the way for several innovative strategies like the use of nanotechnology for the treatment of wounds in diabetic patients. The use of biomaterials, nanomaterials have advanced approaches in tissue engineering by designing multi-functional nanocomposite scaffolds. Stimuli-responsive scaffolds that interact with the wound microenvironment and controlled release of bioactive molecules have helped in overcoming barriers in healing. The use of different types of nanocomposite scaffolds for faster healing of diabetic wounds is constantly being studied. Nanocomposites have helped in addressing specific issues with respect to healing and improving angiogenesis. Method: A literature search was followed to retrieve the articles on strategies for wound healing in diabetes across several databases like PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus and Cochrane database. The search was performed in May 2022 by two researchers independently. They keywords used were “diabetic wounds, nanotechnology, nanocomposites, nanoparticles, chronic diabetic wounds, diabetic foot ulcer, hydrogel”. Exclusion criteria included insulin resistance, burn wound, dressing material. Keywords: nanocomposites, scaffolds, hydrogen-based scaffolds, Chitosan-based scaffolds, diabetic wound healing

sections.text: Nanomedicine is one of the fastest-growing fields offering several avenues for therapy, diagnostics, delivery systems and improving efficiency (1). The superior properties of the ‘nano’ components have been used in tissue engineering for the repair and regeneration of several organs and tissues. Wound healing is a normal process involving a series of steps; however it is affected by a number of variables like age, obesity, stress, diseases, habits, infections, trauma etc. (2). But in certain conditions, healing is halted at the second phase, i.e., the inflammatory phase which could be due to chronic conditions. Many diseases that cause impaired blood flow, such as in the case of diabetic foot ulcers or pressure ulcers are the contributing factors. Common wound pathogens, nosocomial infections are also known to hinder the progression of healing to the third phase, which is proliferation. Several factors are attributed to patients with diabetes mellitus such as the improper function of macrophages and growth factors, and low blood circulation; the major factor for delayed wound healing (3). The incidence of diabetes is seen to be increasing at a steady rate globally, with a mortality rate of 1.5 million deaths in 2019. The indirect death due to diabetes was 460,000 due to kidney disease, and 20% due to cardiovascular complications (4). Diabetic patients are prone to develop diabetic foot ulcers and the percentage affected is more than 20% (5). To treat such chronic wounds, newer therapies such as cell/gene therapy, and engineered biomaterials are sought after due to unsuccessful treatment modalities. Tissue engineering has led researchers to explore several new skin substitutes using natural, synthetic, and semi-synthetic polymers. They are often used in combination with biomolecules, proteins, and polysaccharides (6). To overcome the existing limitations, they have been combined with nanomaterial to form a highly functional, multi-modal, smart nanocomposite to treat chronic wounds such as in the case of diabetes (7). The major advantages of nanotherpay are due to the charge, and large surface area to volume ratio that enhances the interaction with the target area (8). The ability to encapsulate and control the drug release by attaining a sustained release of the desired biomolecules leads to accelerated healing (9). Figure 1 represents the types of nanocomposites and its advantages in wound healing. Various factors, including pH, temperature, blood sugar level, and oxygen saturation, are important in the healing of wounds. Scaffolds have attracted interest recently as a novel dressing and provide an innovative perspective on tissue regeneration (10, 11). Researchers state that the design of the dressing material spatially is of utmost importance for a biomaterial to function as an effective regenerative scaffold, which is now possible through nanocomposites which have been summarised in this review.

sections.section: Nanoparticle based composite scaffold for enhanced healing
sections.text: While researchers are experimenting with effective and scarless wound healing strategies, wound management in diabetes itself is a tedious process for the patients and the healthcare sector. So, several advanced techniques and technology have been employed in the remedial measures for diabetic wounds. Several types of metal nanoparticles, metal oxide nanoparticles, nanotubes, and polymeric nanoparticles have been used in wound healing. Because of their innate antimicrobial property, the silver nanoparticle has been extensively used in wound care management. It is strikingly important to note that silver nanoparticles are effective against nosocomial infections and multidrug-resistant pathogens (12, 13). At a concentration of 50 mg/ml silver nanoparticles were observed to destruct the bacterial cell membrane and kill S. aureus and E. coli (14). A nanocomposite was fabricated with polyethylene glycol diacrylate, silica, bioactive glass nanoparticles, sodium alginate and copper. This silica-based nanocomposite was found to be an excellent injectable with elastomeric, biomimetic, and antibacterial properties. The regeneration of blood vessels was observed with high collagen deposition, and VEGF expression in a full-thickness diabetic wound model (15). Table 1 indicates the different types of nanocomposites employed for diabetic wound healing. Nitric oxide (NO) induces the formation of blood vessels and the migration of endothelial cells by eNOS or MAPk pathways. Zinc oxide is known to induce NO production, hence several scaffolds for wound healing have incorporated ZnO NP’s nanofibers fabricated using poly-caprolactone with ZnO NP’s which exhibited high proliferation of fibroblast cells. A higher rate of vascular regeneration was observed because of the expression of VEGF and FGF (27). Cerium oxide nanoparticles were used in combination with microRNA (miR-146a) for faster healing in diabetic wounds. The synergistic role of scavenging the free radicals and modulating the inflammatory pathway proved to increase the synthesis of collagen, thereby higher rate of angiogenesis and low inflammation; this aided in a significantly higher rate of wound closure (28). Poly-N-acetyl-glucosamine based nanofibrous scaffold was prepared to overcome the limitations in treating a diabetic wound. This bioactive scaffold was found to enhance cell metabolism, and migration of endothelial cells with a higher rate of wound closure in a full- thickness diabetic mice model. The gene expression of uPAR, VEGF, Il-1 and MMP responsible for migration, angiogenesis, inflammatory activity, and matrix remodelling was observed (29). Another study found that short-fibre poly-N-acetyl glucosamine nanofibers were used alongside the vacuum-assisted closure of complex wounds. This aided in controlling the blood loss by acting as a hemostatic agent activating platelets and better granulation. The presence of collagen I and the wound contraction rate was significant in the treated groups (30).

sections.section: Stimuli-responsive scaffold for modulated healing process
sections.text: The ulcers in diabetic wounds are caused by oxidative stress, so researchers prepared Prussian blue nanoparticles (PBNP’s) to scavenge the free radicals generated at the wound site. This PBNP was encapsulated in a heat-sensitive gel using poly (d, L-lactide)-poly (ethylene glycol)-poly (d, L-lactide) (PDLLA-PEG-PDLLA) hydrogel (PLEL). It was confirmed that the nanoparticle was able to protect the cells and mitochondria against reactive oxygen species (ROS). In an animal model, it was found to progress diabetic wound healing at a faster rate, reduce ROS production, and enhance cell survival and growth simultaneously reducing the interleukin and tumor necrosis factor (31). A pH-responsive scaffold was developed which aided in faster healing with less scar formation. This injectable scaffold was prepared with polysaccharides and exhibited antibacterial activity against multi-drug resistant bacteria. In vivo studies showed that the exosome released promoted angiogenesis in the full-thickness wound (32). A dual responsive scaffold that modulates the release based on pH and metformin release was prepared using PEG. The active components encapsulated were phenylboronic acid, benzaldehyde, L-arginine, and chitosan which exhibited anti-inflammatory effects and promoted angiogenesis. The synergistic healing of metformin and graphene oxide was observed in a rat model with type II diabetic foot ulcer. Based on the stimulus it was found to release the drug, metformin which was faster healing in chronic diabetic athletic wounds (33). Silver nanoclusters were conjugated with vancomycin in a gelatin-based hydrogel along with nimesulide that is pH sensitive. This complete biomaterial containing phenylboronic acid and polyvinyl alcohol also contained ROS and exhibited anti-inflammatory action. It was found to be biocompatible, with excellent cell-adhesive behaviour and aided healing in wounds with infection. Because of its sensitive and dual-responsive properties, hydrogel was found to be good for treating chronic diabetic wounds (34). A thermos-responsive scaffold that is skin-friendly and designed for infants and diabetic patients with sensitive skin was attempted by researchers. This non-irritable hydrogel patch was designed with a protein-polyphenol complex that was activated upon reaction to the body temperature upon application. This was found to be skin-friendly and gentle even for a prolonged period of use because of its immune-modulatory action (35).

Hydrogels are the most preferred dressing agent for wound healing owing to their capability to retain moisture at the site of wounds, agent because hydrogels are designed to hold moisture at the wound surface, and create the best setting for healing, balancing skin hydration and in the removal of necrotic tissue. They could be prepared with ease providing sustained drug release. Both natural and synthetic polymers could be used in the preparation of hydrogels. These may include, fibrin, hyaluronic acid, cellulose derivatives, copolymers and others (36). Hydrogels are exceptional in providing a humid atmosphere for the healing of wounds and ensure permeable water vapours with microbial entry prevention at the wound site. A heparinised PVA-based hydrogel formulated demonstrated significant antibacterial activity without any cellular toxic effects (37). Another hydrogel containing coumestrol/hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin was developed using hydroxypropyl methylcellulose. The insoluble coumestrol (helps with photoaging; improves elasticity of skin during menopause) was solubilized using hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin to obtain a hydrogel which led to faster wound healing process through the better propagation of cells. This also demonstrated good cell adhesion and compatibility as observed through Wistar rats (38). A gel-based hydrogel was formulated using adipose-derived stem cells as a suitable wound healing agent that was obtained from both mouse and porcine models. These in vivo models demonstrated excellent healing of wounds (39). Topic nitric oxide helps in the healing process of acute and chronic wounds. An antibacterial peptide was developed based on this, which could self-assemble with respect to changes in pH, and could lead to the development of hydrogel with improved bactericidal activity (40). A ZnO-based nanocomposite hydrogel demonstrated significant antibacterial properties and was found biocompatible and safe with a faster rate of wound healing (41). Though there are many ongoing research on hydrogels related to skin repair, there is another group of researchers who developed hydrogels containing HA and carboxylated CS that mimics skin with high mechanical strength. The in vitro studies on L929 cells demonstrate superior biocompatibility with improved cell proliferation. Further, in vivo studies also demonstrated a faster healing process and suggested that this hydrogel as an ideal candidate suited for wound recovery and healing (42). Though there are many ongoing research on hydrogels used as wound dressing agent, we would like to identify the importance of hydrogels as a potential wound dressing agent with reference to diabetic wounds. Diabetes being a chronic disease is yet challenging to cure and the medical requirements are inadequate (43). The skin wounds caused by diabetes do not get completely healed due to limited blood supply and deprived antimicrobial capability with the poor inflammatory response (44). Among 750,000 emerging cases of diabetic foot ulcer in America, nearly 10% of cases involved amputation of limbs every year (45). Many measures are taken for treating wound healing due to diabetes such as growth factor and cellular-based therapy but the cost was too high (46–48). So, there has been an increasing interest in bioactive biomaterials as a potent wound dressing agent for treating in case of diabetic-based wounds (49). Some of the biomaterials have progressed to clinics such as biomedical hydrogels, films and ointments, and others (50). On the other hand, multifunctional biomaterials are developed with potent antioxidants, antibacterial activity and hemostasis (51–53). Hydrogel biomaterial-based dressings are also developed with their property similar to that of the extracellular matrix and this demonstrated good wound healing (54–58). Due to vascular impairment, diabetes-related wound healing and skin regrowth remain a major concern. To overcome this, a silica-based nanocomposite hydrogel scaffold that could promote both wound healing and skin regeneration in diabetic conditions was developed by enhancing early angiogenesis with no bioactive factors. This injectable nanocomposite exhibits an excellent healing pattern with superior antibacterial properties. Also, enables viability, growth, and angiogenesis of endothelial progenitor cells through in vitro studies. In vivo studies demonstrated restoration of blood vessels through HIF-1α/VEGF and collagen deposition in diabetic wound. It was also suggested to have its application in regenerative medicine (15). Several tissue engineering strategies using nanobiomaterials for vascular regeneration have been reported (59). A multifunctional sprayable cross-linking bioadhesive hydrogel-based nanocomposite was developed for diabetic wound healing. Here, Kappa-carrageenan being the hydrogel matrix, different concentrations of modified ZnO nanoparticles were incorporated to improve their mechanical properties with good antibacterial activity. To this, L-glutamic acid was also loaded into this network to enhance the rate of wound healing. This biocompatible nanocomposite also demonstrated elasticity similar to human skin with adhesive nature and clotting capability. The in vivo studies further demonstrated significant wound healing at a faster rate without any infection (59). A 2-D nanoclay (Laponite RD)/polymer-based nanocomposite hydrogels were developed as a substitute for treating foot ulcers due to diabetes. It was also suggested that enzymes or active compounds loaded to the hydrogel could help in the healing of diabetic foot ulcers through their antibacterial activity (60). Another research on zwitterionic poly (sulfobetaine acrylamide) nanocomposite that was composed of hectorite nanoclay demonstrated as a potent chronic wound dressing agent. This hydrogel exhibited insignificant cytotoxicity against NIH-3T3 fibroblast and was resistant against the adsorption of BSA and certain bacterial strains. In vivo studies on both normal and diabetic wounds were conducted in mice in comparison with commercially available dressings. Histology confirmed significant re-epithelialization and faster healing of diabetic wounds than the commercial products (61). A bioactive HQB nanocomposite hydrogel was developed through the cross-linking of modified hyaluronic acid with quaternized chitosan coated with bioactive glasses. This demonstrated superior wound healing properties in diabetic-induced rats and suggested it to have a good prospect in clinical application (62). A cost-effective and simple dual-network hydrogel comprised of MnO2 nanosheets was developed from silk fibroin and carboxymethyl cellulose. This helped in angiogenesis, reduced inflammation, and had remarkable healing rates comparable to commercial dressing through in vivo studies (63). An alginate and Eudragit nanoparticle-based nanocomposite hydrogel comprising edaravone was produced for the highest ROS sequestration to overcome chronic inflammation and delayed wound healing in diabetes. A lower dosage of this hydrogel enhanced wound healing, and a higher dosage impeded the healing process in diabetic mice and suggested dosage levels played a key role in the healing process (64). Some examples of nanoparticle-based wound dressing materials for which clinical trials are undertaken is listed in Table 2 .

The major risk associated with patients affected with diabetes includes delayed wound healing and amputation. This is mainly due to the reduced tissue blood circulation causing hypoxia and the associated risks. A PVA/Chitosan-based nano fibre wound dressing was developed with high antimicrobial activity, improved vapour transmission rate, good odour-absorbing capacity and no cytotoxic effects; and was proved to accelerate the diabetic wound healing when tested in both diabetic and non-diabetic rats (72). A safe, cyto-compatible, epidermal growth factor-modified curcumin-incorporated chitosan nano-spray was developed that demonstrated accelerated wound healing properties, improved angiogenesis, and re-epithelialization with superior antibacterial effects in rats. It was further suggested that this nano-spray could help in the treatment of diabetic wounds and other skin injuries (73). A formulation composed of poly lactic acid/chitosan nanoscaffolds encapsulating cod liver oil was developed and characterized which demonstrated significant wound healing property to be used in the treatment of the most complicated disorder, diabetic foot ulcers, seen in diabetic patients (74). A topical formulation of lecithin-chitosan nanoparticles incorporated with melatonin was developed with desirable properties such as fibroblast induction, collagen deposition and promotion of angiogenesis. The formulation demonstrated4 accelerated wound closure in diabetic rats (75). A nanocomposite sponge comprised of chitosan, hyaluronic acid and nano-silver was developed against many antibiotic-resistant bacteria including methicillin-resistant S. aureus. The excellent antibacterial action exhibited by this nanocomposite sponge made it a suitable dressing agent for diabetic foot ulcers with mild toxicity towards mammalian cells (76). A hydrogel membrane composed of polyvinyl alcohol, starch, chitosan and nano zinc oxide was prepared and was found effective as a potent wound dressing agent in initial wound healing stages through in vivo studies in rats and exhibited wide-spectrum antibacterial action through in vitro studies (77). An injectable nanocomposite composed of curcumin, chitosan and alginate was identified as a promising wound dressing agent for wound recovery. The in vivo studies in rats demonstrated that the nano-curcumin based nanocomposite showed significant collagen deposition and epidermis re-epithelialization in wounds (78). Although there is a gap in the translation of nanomedicine, the use of computer-aided analysis has become evident in this area. This has led researchers get a clear vision on the behaviour and application of nanoparticle- based therapy in reproductive biology (79), transporting drugs across biological barriers like the blood-brain barrier (80, 81). Another important aspect with respect to the design and use of nanotherapeutics is the toxicity; the understanding of which has been highly enhanced using computational biology (82). Several machine-learning approaches have been explored by the researchers that gives a magnified view of the interaction of the nanomaterial with the cells. This enables tailor-made and non-toxic application of nanomedicine to improve healthcare (83).

Several impeding factors in healing chronic wounds exist using conventional treatment methods. Novel strategies have been designed to overcome them using nanotechnology has proved to be promising. The advanced biomaterials developed with cellular and acellular scaffolds in conjunction with nanomaterials of suitable nature would prove to be an efficient wound care management in diabetic ulcers. The ability to modulate and control the release of active compounds and drugs has added advantage of controlling infection in these wounds significantly shortening the stay at the hospital for patients. An in-depth analysis of the factors that promote angiogenesis and wound closure at a faster rate by the use of nanocomposite biomaterials would help in translating these products to patients. Production of such tailor-made biomaterial constructs with specific factors and design would be the desired wound treatment strategy specifically in chronic wounds. With the recent advancements in the field of artificial intelligence the design of scaffolds could be customised to evade toxicity and meet the scrupulous needs that exist in regenerative therapy. This would help researchers validate and predict the outcome of their research without the sacrifice of many animals, avoid the strain of extraneous tasks involving the toxicological assessment. So, by means of integrating artificial intelligence and the lab-scale studies will yield effective translation of nanotherapeutics in wound care management.

title: A 3R (remove-remodel-repair)-integrated self-assembled Chlorella-gelatin-PEG hydrogel for diabetic wound healing
abstract: Diabetic wound healing remains a critical clinical challenge due to persistent bacterial infections, oxidative stress, and chronic inflammation. Inspired by the principles of traditional Chinese medicine, we developed a multifunctional hydrogel (CPGel) via solvent-driven self-assembly of bioactive Chlorella extracts, gelatin, and polyethylene glycol (PEG). The CPGel synergizes the 3R strategy: (1) Remove—complete eradication of E. coli and S. aureus via intrinsic antibacterial activity; (2) Remodel—65 % ROS scavenging and immunomodulation by polarizing macrophages from proinflammatory M1 to anti-inflammatory M2 phenotypes to resolve chronic inflammation; and (3) Repair—accelerated tissue regeneration via 9-fold angiogenesis (α-SMA) and 2-fold collagen I deposition. Mechanically robust (compressive strength: 4.16 MPa; tensile strength: 627 kPa) and antifreezing (−100 °C), CPGel demonstrated exceptional transparency and adhesion, ensuring seamless integration with wound sites. In diabetic mice, CPGel achieved 100 % wound closure within 21 days, surpassing controls (73 %), while promoting neovascularization and hair follicle regeneration. This study bridges traditional herbal medicine with advanced biomaterial engineering, offering a scalable, toxin-free platform that addresses the triad of diabetic wound pathogenesis. By harmonizing the 3R strategy-Remove, Remodel, and Repair-CPGel represents a paradigm shift in chronic wound management, with high potential for clinical translation and sustainable therapeutic design. sections.text: Diabetes is a common chronic disease affecting more than 400 million individuals worldwide [1]. Approximately 25 % of diabetic patients face the serious complication of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs). The hospitalization rate of DFU patients was 55 % higher than that of those without ulcers. Over 50 % of DFU patients need surgical intervention. Even after successful treatment, the first-year recurrence rate remains at 40 % [2,3]. Diabetic wound healing is hindered by chronic inflammation related to diabetes. This causes the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and creates an inflammatory environment at the wound site. In this area, inflammatory macrophages (M1 phenotype) persist but do not shift to the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype [4,5]. This results in an environment that is unfavourable for tissue regeneration, thereby inhibiting wound healing by damaging fibroblast proliferation and vascular network repair due to oxidative stress and proinflammatory cytokines [6,7]. Furthermore, patients with diabetes more frequently develop bacterial infections, exacerbating the healing environment [8,9]. Therefore, there is an urgent need for advanced therapeutic approaches capable of combating bacterial infections, alleviating inflammation, regulating ROS, enhancing revascularization, and promoting wound healing. Hydrogels are soft and have high porosity, allowing for oxygen/carbon dioxide and nutrient exchange. They also maintain a moist environment that aids healing. This is why they are often chosen for treating diabetic wounds [10]. Adding bioactive substances such as antibiotics, growth factors, and cells to hydrogels helps create composite hydrogels that accelerate wound healing [11,12]. However, the use of different materials also increases the risk of causing cell inflammation and toxicity [11]. Moreover, the synthesis of these hydrogels is complex and costly, which makes clinical use difficult [5,13]. There is a pressing need to develop a multifunctional hydrogel dressing that is cost-effective and easy to produce. Researchers have noted the many benefits of natural bioactive substances from Chinese herbal medicines. These substances can help heal chronic wounds [14,15]. Research shows that phenolic compounds, polypeptides, and fatty acids have anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, antioxidant, and angiogenesis-promoting effects [[16], [17], [18]]. Chlorella is a green microalga made up of one cell. It is often a key ingredient in health products and medicines. This is due to its remarkable safety, high value, and low cost [19]. Recently, Chlorella has attracted increasing interest. Its high levels of protein, lipids, vitamins, and pigments provide various benefits. These effects include anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, immunomodulatory, and hypoglycemic effects [[20], [21], [22], [23]]. Additionally, Chlorella has a rapid growth rate and has low requirements for the growth environment. As a result, its annual production volume in multiple countries has reached thousands of tons [20]. Current Chlorella extraction techniques (supercritical CO2 [24], freeze-thaw [25], enzymatic lysis [26]) face limitations in scalability due to high costs and complexity. The key challenge lies in optimizing simple, cost-effective protocols that retain biocompatibility and bioactivity for clinically viable hydrogel dressings. Polyethylene glycol (PEG) is a key hydrophilic polymer. It has played a vital role in biomedical applications for more than twenty years. PEG is commonly found in medical devices, health products, and cosmetics [27]. Renowned for its excellent water solubility, stability, biodegradability, and low immunogenicity, it has received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) [28,29]. Furthermore, PEG has a flexible structure with two terminal hydroxyl groups. This property allows it to effectively increase the solubility of hydrophobic compounds through intermolecular forces. Thus, different compounds can be extracted from Chinese herbal medicines. This includes both hydrophilic compounds, such as polysaccharides and proteins, and hydrophobic compounds, such as fatty acids and pigments [[30], [31], [32]]. The hydrophilic chain segments in PEG endow hydrogels with excellent ductility, flexibility, elasticity, and mechanical properties. [33]. In addition, PEG is among the most commonly used polymers for designing injectable hydrogels [34]. The terminal hydroxyl groups in its structure can create self-assembled hydrogels. This happens through intermolecular interactions. This preparation method requires no structural modification or addition of small-molecule toxic cross-linkers [11]. Gelatin is a polypeptide derived from collagen. It includes various functional groups, such as terminal α-amino groups, carboxyl groups from aspartic acid, and ε-amino groups from lysine. These groups can bond with hydroxyl groups through hydrogen bonds [35]. Furthermore, its RGD sequence has functions similar to those of natural ECM. This makes it an important option for preparing wound dressings. However, its quick breakdown, weak mechanical properties, fast water loss, and high risk of bacteria limit its clinical use [35,36]. Inspired by the synergy of traditional Chinese medicine and biomaterials, we engineered CPGel through PEG/water-mediated extraction of Chlorella bioactive compounds and self-assembly with gelatin (Scheme 1). Unlike conventional hydrogels, CPGel employs non-covalent interactions to integrate three therapeutic axes: Remove (antimicrobial compounds for bacterial clearance), Remodel (ROS scavenging and M2 macrophage polarization to resolve inflammation), and Repair (angiogenesis and collagen remodelling). By addressing the triad of diabetic wound pathogenesis—infection, oxidative stress, and impaired regeneration—CPGel embodies a paradigm shift in wound care, merging herbal efficacy with engineered material performance. This 3R strategy not only simplifies clinical translation but also aligns with sustainable, patient-centric therapeutic design.Scheme 1Molecular engineering and therapeutic mechanism of the CPGel hydrogel for diabetic wound healing. (a) Dynamic hydrogen bonds between gelatine's carboxyl groups, PEG chains, and bioactive compounds in Chlorella extract drive three-dimensional network formation. (b) The hydrogel has antifreeze, water-retaining, tissue-adhesive, strong mechanical, and injectable properties. (c) The hydrogel dressing performs multiple therapeutic functions through sustained bioactive components: scavenging bacteria, reducing reactive oxygen species, inhibiting inflammation, and promoting collagen deposition, vascular regeneration and hair follicle neogenesis.Scheme 1

sections.section: Preparation, structure, and gelation time of CPGel hydrogels
sections.text: In traditional Chinese medicine, the classic processing method involves decocting traditional Chinese medicine with a suitable solvent [16]. Through the diffusion action of the solvent, it penetrates cells, dissolves soluble substances, creates a concentration difference inside and outside the cells, and extracts the active ingredients from the herbal tissues [37]. Therefore, we employed the classic solvent decoction method to prepare a traditional Chinese herbal medicine-based hydrogel (Fig. 1A). In brief, the active components of Chlorella are extracted using PEG and H2O at 80 °C for 4 h. Gelatin was first dissolved in CV under continuous stirring at 60 °C, followed by the addition of the CE solution with sustained agitation. When the homogeneous mixture was allowed to cool to 37 °C, the CPGel hydrogel formed immediately, demonstrating its in situ polymerization characteristics. This phenomenon arises from gelatin being a composite of polypeptide chains with diverse molecular weights resulting from collagen degradation. When exposed to temperature variations (lower temperatures), polypeptide chains undergo cross-linking propelled by both hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions [38].Fig. 1Preparation, structure, and gelation time of CPGel hydrogels. (A) Schematic diagram of CPGel hydrogel synthesis. (B) UV spectra of the Chlorella PEG extract. (C) UV spectra of the Chlorella H2O extract. (D) Optical images of the gelation progress of the CPGel hydrogel (I, III). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of the hydrogels (Ⅱ, IV); scale bars: 100 μm.Fig. 1 The effective extraction of various active components from Chlorella using PEG and H2O serves as a fundamental cornerstone for the success of this work [24,25]. Hence, the composition of the extracts was analysed via ultraviolet spectroscopy (Fig. 1B–C). The H2O extract exhibited a maximum absorption peak near 267 nm, whereas the maximum absorption peaks for nucleic acid, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, and protein were detected at 260, 259, 278, 279, and 280 nm, respectively [[39], [40], [41]]. These findings indicate the successful extraction of one or more aromatic amino acids, proteins, or nucleic acids. Additionally, a maximum absorption peak at approximately 210 nm was observed [42], indicating the presence of peptide molecules. Furthermore, small absorption peaks were detected at approximately 410, 660 and 640 nm, suggesting the presence of chlorophyll and lutein [43]. Some absorption peaks were also observed at 240 nm and 310 nm. The characteristic peaks for aromatic amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids, and peptides exhibited a blueshift in the longwave direction due to the presence of -OH groups in PEG, which caused the absorption peaks of unsaturated bonds to shift toward shorter wavelengths [31]. Notably, strong absorption peaks were observed at 410 nm and 660 nm, whereas small peaks were observed in the range of 500–600 nm, indicating that the extraction of pigments from Chlorella via PEG was more effective than that from H2O. The terminal hydroxyl groups of PEG synergistically interact with the active components of Chlorella Extract (such as the amino groups of polysaccharides) to form hydrogen bonds with 18 amino acid residues in gelatin, establishing a temperature-responsive network that positively contributes to CPGel hydrogel application as a wound dressing. When the PEG content reached 46 % of the liquid phase, the CPGel hydrogel did not flow when inverted at 37 °C (Fig. 1D I and III). Therefore, our experimental design consists of five groups: Gel, PGel (variants 1, 2, and 3), and CPGel hydrogels. The time required for gelation was meticulously documented via the small bottle inversion technique, as delineated in Fig. S1. We found that the gelation time of the CPGel hydrogel (75 ± 2.5 s) was 3.3 times faster than that of PGel-2 and 1.9 times faster than that of PGel-3. The experimental results demonstrated that the integration of PEG and Chlorella effectively improved the ability of the Gel hydrogel to achieve gelation at 37 °C. Simultaneously, the active constituents within Chlorella, including amino acids, proteins, and pigments, contribute additional hydrogen-bonding interactions during the sol‒gel transition of the CPGel hydrogel. The presence of these active components thereby promotes further physical entanglement within the three-dimensional network structure of the CPGel hydrogel, potentially enhancing its overall stability and functionality. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) revealed that after the addition of PEG and Chlorella, the walls of the hydrogel were noticeably thicker than those of the Gel hydrogel were (Fig. 1D Ⅱ and Ⅳ). Moreover, the CPGel hydrogel displays an interconnected macroporous network structure (Fig. S2). This unique structure facilitates the infiltration of nutrients and the transport of water and blood, factors that are highly important for the wound healing process [44].

sections.section: The injectability, transparency, and adhesion properties of hydrogels
sections.text: In the field of biomedical research, interest among dedicated researchers in the development of injectable adhesive hydrogels has significantly increased in recent years [23]. This heightened attention can be attributed to the myriad of benefits these hydrogels offer, such as the convenience of drug administration via syringes, the ability to undergo gelation through dynamic bonding mechanisms, and their unique capacity to reinstate the original mechanical characteristics of the gel upon the skin's surface [24,25]. The CPGel hydrogel demonstrated in situ polymerization through the hydrophilic groups of collagen [26], the hydroxyl groups at the ends of the PEG chains [32], and the pharmacological components of the Chlorella extracts (Fig. 2A).Fig. 2The injectability, transparency, and adhesiveness properties of the hydrogels. (A) Schematic diagram of hydrogel injectability. (B) Schematic diagram of the interface interactions between the hydrogels and tissue. (C) Photographs of the CPGel hydrogels showing their adhesion, injectability, and various shapes. (D) The hydrogels adhered to porcine skin, and no residue was found after peeling. (E) Adhesiveness of the hydrogels. (F) Images showing the transparency of the hydrogel. (G) UV–Vis absorbance of the hydrogels.Fig. 2 Thus, we predict that during the CPGel sol-gel process, when it is injected through a syringe, these components are highly likely to form strong hydrogen bonds with the hydrophilic groups on the skin mucosa/tissues (Fig. 2B). Consequently, it can adhere to the wound area on the skin. This remarkable characteristic inspired us to further explore the potential of the CPGel hydrogel as a high-performance wound dressing. The syringe containing the CPGel hydrogel was removed from the incubator at 60 °C and gently extruded through the plunger. The CPGel hydrogel demonstrated the expected attributes of localized targeting (Fig. 2C I, II, III). Excitingly, the CPGel hydrogel demonstrated the remarkable ability to establish reversible adhesion on the material surface within a few seconds after injection (Fig. Supporting Moving 1). The CPGel hydrogel was subjected to repeated bending and twisting, and the results demonstrated the robustness of the internal structure of the CPGel hydrogel while tightly adhering to the skin surface (Fig. 2D). Compared with Gel hydrogels, both PGel and CPGel hydrogels boast higher concentrations of -NH2, -COOH, and -OH (Fig. 2E). This enriched composition not only enhances their affinity for the skin but also imparts them with significantly stronger adhesive strength [45]. These observations are crucial for clinical applications, ensuring that the CPGel hydrogel does not solidify too quickly or too slowly at ambient temperature, preventing premature solidification within the syringe or failure to stay at the wound site. Additionally, it can be effectively integrated with skin tissues, avoiding the need for excessive material design. Furthermore, the CPGel hydrogel effortlessly adhered to tissues through physical crosslinking, leaving no residue when peeled off from pig skin (Fig. 2D). This feature offers significant convenience in clinical applications, as it not only reduces the discomfort patients may feel during dressing changes but also alleviates the mental burden on healthcare professionals who must apply dressings with precision. We observed that the CPGel hydrogel exhibited remarkable shape adaptability, allowing it to be molded into diverse forms, such as flowers, rabbits, and hearts (Fig. 2C Ⅳ), while maintaining its transparency. Notably, the Gel and PGel-2 hydrogels were placed on a university emblem, displaying a clearly visible pattern (Fig. 2F). However, excessive PEG concentrations induced gelatin precipitation, resulting in opaque PGel-3 hydrogels with 0 % transmittance. Therefore, hydrogels prepared with PEG solutions at concentrations no greater than 56 % demonstrate greater potential for personalized treatment and real-time monitoring.

sections.section: Mechanical properties, water retention and anti-freezing properties of CPGel hydrogels
sections.text: Achieving a delicate balance between injectability and mechanical properties that are compatible with skin tissues is a challenging task in the field of biomedical tissue engineering [28]. The unique composition of the CPGel hydrogel, which is based on a multicomponent solvent system with extended functionality, allows the introduction of multiple interaction sites into the polymer network system. These interaction sites include the hydroxyl groups of flexible PEG and the abundant aromatic rings, phenolic hydroxyl groups, and carboxyl groups found in microalgal extracts. This characteristic prompted us to explore the compatibility of the mechanical properties of the CPGel hydrogel with skin tissues. To evaluate the mechanical stability of different components of the hydrogels, we conducted oscillatory frequency sweep tests [29] (Fig. 3A). The storage modulus (G′) of the CPGel hydrogel is ten times greater than the loss modulus (G″), and it remains relatively constant within the 0.1–10 % strain range. This finding indicates that the CPGel hydrogel predominantly exhibits elastic behavior [46], similar to the remarkable elasticity observed in soft tissues of the skin [30]. The addition of Chlorella extract and PEG improved the energy storage modulus of the hydrogels, suggesting that the CPGel could effectively adapt to the wound site and enhance their suitability for wound healing.Fig. 3The mechanical properties, water retention and antifreezing properties of the CPGel hydrogels. (A) Hydrogel energy storage and loss moduli. (B) Hydrogel strain and compression stress curves. (C) Cyclic tensile load‒unloading curves of the CPGel hydrogels. (D) Curves of tensile stress and strain for hydrogels. (E) DSC curves of the hydrogels (from −100 to 40 °C). (F) Plots of weight loss for the hydrogels. (n = 3). (G) Photographs of the hydrogels at −20 °C and −80 °C. (H) Tensile, torsional, and bending diagrams of the hydrogel at room temperature for 24 h.Fig. 3 Furthermore, an ideal wound dressing hydrogel should adhere tightly to the skin, maintaining stable elastic properties even in the face of unpredictable external forces and patient movements [31]. To evaluate this, we utilized a universal mechanical tester to gradually compress the 2 cm hydrogel to 0.4 cm. The structural integrity of the hydrogel groups was maintained at a testing rate of 50 mm/min at 80 % strain. Notably, the compressive strength increased with the addition of PEG and Chlorella extract. Notably, the compressive strength of the CPGel hydrogel reached 4.16 ± 0.012 MPa, which was eight times greater than that of the Gel hydrogel (0.52 ± 0.005 MPa) (Fig. 3B, Fig. S3A). Additionally, during testing, the CPGel hydrogel exhibited resilience. The gel hydrogel was compressed repeatedly, resulting in hydrogel cracking, whereas the PGel-2 and CPGel hydrogels returned to their original state and could be squeezed repeatedly (Fig. S4). Further investigations involved cyclic loading‒unloading experiments on CPGel hydrogels at a strain of 60 %. The results depicted in Fig. 3C demonstrated that while the compression process after the initial rebound resulted in energy dissipation, the subsequent four compression‒rebound cycles stabilized, indicating the fatigue resistance of the CPGel hydrogel [47]. Moreover, we conducted standard dumbbell-shaped tensile strain measurements on the hydrogel samples (Fig. S3B). The hydrophilicity of PEG enables it to insert between protein chains, thereby enhancing their interactions [30]. The addition of PEG significantly increased the maximum tensile stress of the hydrogel, with the PGel-2 hydrogel exhibiting a tensile strength of 439 ± 9.1 kPa, approximately 15 times greater than that of the Gel hydrogel (19 ± 1.0 kPa) (Fig. 3D). The tensile strengths of the PGel-3 and PGel-1 hydrogels were 257 ± 3.2 kPa and 98 ± 1.2 kPa, respectively (Fig. S3C), indicating varying degrees of improvement in tensile strength. Additionally, the incorporation of Chlorella extract enhanced the tensile performance of the hydrogel, with the CPGel hydrogel demonstrating a tensile strength exceeding 627 ± 2.7 kPa, which is 33 times greater than that of the Gel hydrogel (19 ± 1.0 kPa) and 1.4 times greater than that of the PGel-2 hydrogel. The fracture elongation of the CPGel hydrogel increased from 66 ± 5 % (Gel hydrogel) to 177 ± 10 %, whereas the fracture capacities of PGel-3, PGel-2, and PGel-1 reached 142 ± 8 %, 206 ± 12 %, and 142 ± 7 %, respectively. This phenomenon occurs when PEG is inserted between collagen polymer chains, weakening the physical bonds between polymer molecules, increasing the free space between them, and allowing for molecular chain movement and enhanced flexibility. Moreover, in addition to the molecular interactions with the hydrogel chains, PEG also forms strong hydrogen bonds with H2O molecules, effectively influencing the crystallization temperature and evaporation rate of H2O (Fig. 3E–G). We investigated the stability of the hydrogels at lower temperatures by placing them in −20 °C and −80 °C refrigerators for 24 h (Fig. 3G). The freezing resistance of the hydrogels significantly improved with increasing PEG content. To further analyse the freezing resistance of the hydrogels, we used differential scanning calorimetry at −100 °C–40 °C. The freezing resistance of the PGel hydrogels improved significantly with increasing PEG content. No crystallization peak was observed in the DSC curves of the PGel-3 and PGel-2 hydrogels, indicating their remarkable resistance to extreme temperatures. Moreover, the addition of Chlorella extract did not compromise freezing resistance, and the CPGel hydrogel remained soft even at −100 °C. This greatly expands the potential application of CPGel hydrogels as wound dressings, as most hydrogels tend to freeze below 0 °C, resulting in their hardening and loss of moisture, which is detrimental to wound healing [32]. Maintaining adequate water retention at different temperatures is crucial for sustaining a moist wound environment, facilitating the breakdown of necrotic tissue, and promoting wound healing [33]. Changes in the weights of the hydrogels were monitored over a 4-day period under open-air conditions (Fig. 3F). A higher specific gravity of PEG led to better water retention. The mass of the PGel-3 hydrogel remained constant, whereas the PGel-2 hydrogel and PGel-1 hydrogels retained 70 % and 55 % of their initial weights, respectively. In contrast, the mass of the Gel hydrogels decreased by 80 % after just one day, resulting in compromised mechanical properties such as the inability to stretch, bend, or twist (Fig. 3H). There was almost no difference in water retention between the CPGel hydrogel and PGel-2 hydrogel. Multifunctional injectable hydrogels hold immense promise for a wide array of clinical applications and are appealing minimally invasive therapeutic options. However, conventional multifunctional injectable hydrogels are frequently characterized by their intricate preparation processes and suboptimal mechanical robustness. Inevitably, hydrogels must withstand mechanical stresses throughout the wound healing process. In this study, the use of polyethylene glycol as a solvent introduces numerous binding sites and enhances the mechanical strength of the material. Concurrently, the self-assembled CPGel hydrogel sustains the dynamic attributes of the hydrogel. This innovative concept, wherein the solvent functions as a "cross-linker", potentially offers a versatile strategy for the clinical development of hydrogels. This technique adeptly overcomes the challenge of reconciling the dual requirements of injectability and mechanical resilience, thereby advancing the prospects of hydrogel-based therapies in clinical practice.

sections.section: In vitro antibacterial activity of CPGel hydrogels
sections.text: Diabetic wounds, known for their slow healing process, often produce more exudate than other wounds do, increasing the risk of bacterial infection [34,35]. Therefore, dressings with inherent antibacterial properties are crucial. In this study, we initially used a plate method to assess the inhibitory ability of the hydrogel against both gram-negative bacteria (E. coli) and gram-positive bacteria (S. aureus). As shown in Fig. 4A and B, no bacterial colonies were observed on CE, PGel, or CPGel hydrogels, indicating that both PEG and CE exhibit strong antibacterial effects. Furthermore, the growth curve shown in Fig. 4C revealed no inhibition of bacterial growth in the control group, whereas bacterial growth was nearly completely inhibited in the PGel hydrogel, CE, and CPGel hydrogel groups, confirming the potent antibacterial activity of these materials. We hypothesize that the high PEG content in the hydrogel dressing led to a low water content in the in vitro bacterial environment, ultimately resulting in bacterial death due to water loss [36]. Additionally, the robust antimicrobial properties of CE can be attributed to the presence of substances such as antimicrobial peptides, polyphenols, and unsaturated fatty acids [37].Fig. 4The hydrogels exhibited antibacterial properties in vitro. (A) Photographs of the bacterial colony formation assay. (B) Antibacterial ratios of the bacterial colonies were calculated. (C) Growth curve of bacteria after hydrogel treatment. (D) Photographs of representative morphologies of E. coli and S. aureus after hydrogel treatment. The data are presented as the means ± SDs (n = 3). ∗P < 0.05; ∗∗P < 0.01; ∗∗∗P < 0.001.Fig. 4 To further validate our findings, we used field emission electron microscopy (FESEM) to examine the morphology and integrity of the bacteria following treatment with the hydrogels (Fig. 4D). Bacteria treated with Gel hydrogels and the control group exhibited normal cell morphology and intact cell walls. In contrast, bacteria treated with PGel hydrogels displayed noticeable shrinkage, whereas those treated with the CE and CPGel hydrogels presented severe damage to their cell walls. These observations provide compelling evidence of the formidable antibacterial capabilities inherent in CPGel hydrogels. This underscores their promising potential to serve as efficacious wound dressings, offering a formidable defense against bacterial infections.

The biocompatibility of a material is an essential prerequisite for its application as a wound dressing, ensuring that it interacts harmoniously with the biological environment without eliciting adverse reactions or compromising the healing process [38]. To assess the biocompatibility of the CPGel hydrogels, we directly inoculated NIH/3T3 cells onto the hydrogels and performed live/dead staining after 24 h. As shown in Fig. 5A, no significant cytotoxic effects were observed across all experimental groups, with cell viability exceeding 80 % at all tested concentrations. Notably, CPGel exhibited a dose-dependent pro-proliferative effect, as evidenced by the 130 % viability at 416.7 μg/mL (Fig. 5B). This enhanced cellular response likely stems from CPGel's bioactive components. The sustained biocompatibility further validates its suitability for prolonged wound healing applications.Fig. 5The biocompatibility of the hydrogels. (A) Live/dead fluorescence results of NIH-3T3 fibroblasts after hydrogel treatment for 24 h. (B) Viability of NIH-3T3 fibroblasts treated with various concentrations of the hydrogels. (C) H&E-stained organ sections after hydrogel treatment. Scale bars: 100 μm. (D) Hepatic function parameters and (E) renal function parameters. ∗P < 0.05, ∗∗P < 0.01, ∗∗∗P < 0.001. The data are presented as the means ± SDs (n = 6).Fig. 5 Furthermore, we assessed the in vivo toxicity of the hydrogels by analysing their biochemical parameters and histology. As shown in Fig. 5C, the hearts, kidneys, lungs, spleens, and livers of all the mice treated with the hydrogels presented the same morphological characteristics as those of the control group did, with no signs of pathological changes (Fig. 5C–E). The exceptional biocompatibility of the CPGel hydrogels can be attributed to the fact that all the materials used in the preparation process are FDA-approved and devoid of any potentially toxic chemical agents. These results provide evidence that CE and CPGel hydrogels have the potential to serve as effective and safe wound dressings, promoting optimal wound healing.

sections.section: In vitro ROS-scavenging activity and anti-inflammatory effects of CPGel hydrogels
sections.text: Elevated levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation are commonly observed in diabetic wounds because of persistent high blood sugar, infection, and an activated immune system. This oxidative stress significantly contributes to chronic inflammation and delayed wound healing [48]. In the absence of CPGel hydrogels, cell survival reached 70 % at a H2O2 concentration of 700 μM (Fig. S5A). However, with the addition of CPGel, cell viability increased significantly in a dose-dependent manner, with the highest cell viability observed in the groups treated with higher concentrations (24.3 and 72.9 μg/mL). Our comprehensive analysis the predominant antioxidant activity is predominantly attributed to the rich polysaccharide content within Chlorella [25,49]. The primary reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated by cells during trauma and injury include hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and superoxide anions [50]. In mammalian cells, the major antioxidant enzymes responsible for breaking down superoxide anions and H2O2 are superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase, respectively [13]. To assess the simulated SOD activity of the CPGel hydrogel, we utilized a xanthine/xanthine oxidase reaction system to measure the degradation of superoxide radicals. the CPGel hydrogel demonstrated a superoxide radical scavenging efficiency of 60 %, markedly surpassing for PGel (35 %) and CE (45 %). This enhanced radical scavenging capability correlated with its H2O2 degradation capacity, suggesting a robust antioxidative ability in CPGel. To evaluate the intracellular ROS levels, we employed 2′,7′-dichlorofluorescin diacetate (DCFH-DA) as a fluorescent probe. Upon H2O2 stimulation, an increase in the intracellular fluorescence signal, corresponding to elevated levels of intracellular ROS, was observed (Fig. 6A). However, in the presence of the CPGel hydrogel, the fluorescence signal was significantly reduced, indicating the strong ROS scavenging activity of the CPGel hydrogel. Overall, the CPGel hydrogel demonstrated potent antioxidative activity, as evidenced by its ability to scavenge ROS and SOD. In contrast, the PGel hydrogels and CE exhibited moderate antioxidation activity, suggesting that the combination of PGel and Chlorella could have synergistic antioxidative effects.Fig. 6Anti-inflammatory activity and ROS scavenging activity of the CPGel hydrogel in vitro. (A) Antioxidant activity of the hydrogels. Influence of CPGel hydrogels on the expression of CD86 (B), IL-1β (C), TNF-α (D), CD206 (E), IL-10 (F) and TGF-β (G) in LPS-activated RAW264.7 cells. The data are presented as the means ± SDs (n = 3). ∗P < 0.05; ∗∗P < 0.01; ∗∗∗P < 0.001.Fig. 6 Macrophages can exhibit either proinflammatory or anti-inflammatory functions, depending on their role in tissue remodelling. The “alternatively activated” M2 macrophages regulate the immune system, whereas the “classically activated” M1 macrophages promote inflammation [51]. Wound dressings that can promote the transition from the M1 phenotype to the M2 phenotype are advantageous for managing chronic wounds. To evaluate the in vitro anti-inflammatory effects of PGel hydrogels, CEs, and CPGel hydrogels, we used lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated RAW 264.7 macrophages, a commonly used method to induce macrophage inflammatory responses [10]. Following LPS stimulation, the expression of proinflammatory cytokines (CD86, IL-1β, and TNF-α) significantly increased in macrophages. However, treatment with the PGel, CE, or CPGel hydrogels significantly suppressed the expression of these proinflammatory cytokines in LPS-treated RAW264.7 cells, with the CPGel hydrogels demonstrating the most profound inhibitory effect (Fig. 6B–D). Furthermore, CPGel hydrogel treatment resulted in the highest expression of anti-inflammatory genes (CD206, IL-10, and TGF-β) among all the groups (Fig. 6E–G), the superior anti-inflammatory properties of the CPGel hydrogel are attributed to the synergistic effects of polar lipids [52], polysaccharides [53], pigments [54], and proteins [54] within the Chlorella. These results imply that the application of CPGel hydrogels not only suppresses the expression of proinflammatory cytokines within macrophages but also actively promotes the polarization of these cells toward the M2 phenotype. Consequently, our findings suggest that CPGel hydrogels exert immunosuppressive effects by facilitating the shift toward M2 macrophage polarization. This mechanism likely plays a pivotal role in mitigating the inflammatory response and thereby enhancing the progression of diabetic wound healing.

sections.section: In vivo wound healing in a full-thickness skin defect model
sections.text: To assess the effectiveness of CPGel hydrogels as wound dressings, a study was conducted on the healing of whole skin defects in mice (Fig. 7A). The CPGel, CE, and PGel hydrogels were injected into 6-mm-diameter wounds on the backs of the mice, with a blank group treated with PBS serving as the control group. The wounds were observed for 21 days. As time progressed after the operation, the size of the wound area gradually decreased in all four groups (Fig. 7B). After 7 days of therapy, the trauma area in the PGel hydrogel, CE, and CPGel hydrogel groups was significantly smaller than that in the control group (P < 0.05). After 14 days of therapy, the trauma areas in the CE group (61 %) and CPGel hydrogel group (71 %) were substantially different from those in the blank group (41 %). On day 21, complete wound healing (100 %) was observed in the CPGel hydrogel treatment group, whereas wounds persisted in the other groups (with wound healing rates of 73 % in the PBS group, 82 % in the PGel hydrogel group, and 92 % in the CE group) (Fig. 7C, Fig. S6). These results highlight the significant impact of CE on the healing of diabetic wounds and further demonstrate that the synergistic release of CE into PGel hydrogels greatly accelerates the process of wound repair.Fig. 7CPGel hydrogels in diabetic wound repair. (A) Diagram of the wound healing procedure. (B) Representative images of the process of wound healing at 0, 7, 14, and 21 days. (C) Simulation diagram of the wound healing process. (D) Histological analysis of the wound (blood vessels: red arrows; boundary of the epithelium: blue lines; hair follicles: yellow arrows). Scale bar: 200 μm. (E) Epidermal thickness of the wound. (F) Quantification of blood vessels in the wound. (G) Masson's trichrome staining. Scale bars: 200 μm. (H) Quantification of hair follicles in the wound. (I) Quantification of collagen remodelling. Scale bars: 50 μm. The data are presented as the means ± SDs (n = 6). (For interpretation of the references to color in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the Web version of this article.)Fig. 7 To further investigate the effectiveness of CPGel hydrogels in promoting the regeneration of skin tissue, wound tissues at different time points were subjected to hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and Masson's trichrome staining. H&E staining revealed that the wounds treated with CPGel hydrogels not only exhibited faster healing but also exhibited skin attachments in the scar area (Fig. 7D). Additionally, on day 7, the epidermal thickness in the CPGel hydrogel group was significantly greater than that in the other groups (P < 0.05) (Fig. 7E). Furthermore, at 14 days, the CPGel hydrogel group presented a greater number of blood vessels than did the other three groups. Notably, at 21 days, the number of blood vessels in the CPGel hydrogel group was twice as high as that in the blank group (P < 0.05) (Fig. 7F). This result provides biological evidence supporting the ability of CPGel hydrogels to promote wound repair, as neovascularization plays a crucial role in providing essential nutrients and oxygen to the damaged tissue microenvironment, ultimately facilitating wound healing [19]. Furthermore, the number of hair follicles in the skin tissue of the CE (367 %) and CPGel (533 %) hydrogel treatment groups was significantly greater than that in the skin tissue of the PGel (167 %) and blank (100 %) hydrogel groups (P < 0.05) (Fig. 7H). This finding further confirms the remarkable potential of CPGel hydrogels in promoting wound repair. Furthermore, the results of Masson staining are presented in Fig. 7G. On day 7, the blank group presented a shallow blue color, indicating limited collagen deposition. In contrast, collagen deposition was evident in the PGel hydrogel, CE hydrogel, and CPGel hydrogel groups. As time progressed, collagen deposition increased in all the groups, but the CP gel hydrogel and CE groups presented significantly faster collagen deposition than did the PGel hydrogel and blank groups did (resulting in a deeper blue color). Additionally, picrosirius red staining was employed to assess the maturation of newly formed skin tissues after treatment with CPGel hydrogels, and the results are presented in Fig. S7. Remarkable deposition of collagen I was observed in the CPGel hydrogel group, which significantly differed from that in the other three groups and was twice as high as that in the blank group (Fig. 7I). In contrast, the blank control group and PGel hydrogel group predominantly exhibited immature collagen type III deposition. These findings indicate that CPGel hydrogels could be beneficial for facilitating collagen remodelling and skin maturation.

sections.section: Effects of hydrogels on epidermal differentiation, neovascularization, and inflammation in diabetic wound healing
sections.text: Research on wound therapy has consistently demonstrated that a deficiency in angiogenesis at the wound site presents a formidable obstacle, often resulting in impaired wound healing [55]. Consequently, to evaluate the angiogenic response in the treated wound tissues, we conducted immunofluorescence staining for α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) and CD31, two key markers of angiogenesis. The expression of α-SMA and CD31 in the CPGel hydrogel group was significantly different from that in the other three groups (Fig. 8A–C). Specifically, the expression of α-SMA was nine times greater than that in the control group and three times greater than that in the CE group. These findings indicate that the CPGel hydrogel has a better ability to promote angiogenesis in the target area, effectively induces angiogenesis and neovascularization, ensures sufficient blood supply to the injured area, and facilitates the exchange of oxygen and nutrients during the process of wound healing, thus promoting good healing of the wound.Fig. 8Immunofluorescence analyses of diabetic wounds after treatment for 7 days. (A) Staining for α-SMA and CD31. The white arrows indicate positive expression in small arteries. (B) Number of small α-SMA-positive arteries. (C) Percentage of CD31-positive areas. Immunofluorescence staining results of (D) CD86, CD206, TNF-α (red) and IL-1β (red) are presented; scale bars: 100 μm. Images were analysed to quantify the percentage of areas positive for (E) CD86, (F) CD 206, (G) IL-1β and (H) TNF-α expression. The data are presented as the means ± SDs (n = 6). ∗P < 0.05; ∗∗P < 0.01; ∗∗∗P < 0.001. (For interpretation of the references to color in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the Web version of this article.)Fig. 8 CE has been shown to be effective in reducing inflammation and modulating the immune system [56]. Combined with the in vitro finding that the CP gel reduced M1-type macrophage activation, we further investigated whether the reduced inflammation and improved healing of diabetic wounds were related to the polarized state of macrophages. First, we performed immunostaining to detect CD86 (M1)- and CD206 (M2)-positive cells (Fig. 8D). Interestingly, none of the treatment groups presented visibly more CD86-positive regions than the other groups did. However, a significant decrease in CD86 expression was observed in the CPGel hydrogel group (Fig. 8E). Similarly, none of the treatment groups presented significantly fewer CD206-positive regions than the other groups did. In contrast, the CPGel hydrogel group presented elevated CD206 expression (Fig. 8F). In addition, external intervention during inflammation is essential during diabetic wound healing. The amount of proinflammatory cytokines serves as an important indicator of the degree of inflammation. Therefore, we conducted staining for TNF-α and IL-1β (Fig. 8D), two proinflammatory cytokines secreted by proinflammatory macrophages that are associated with delayed diabetic wound healing. After treatment with the CPGel, the expression of TNF-α and IL-1β in the central area of the wound was significantly reduced (Fig. 8G and H). Although TNF-α expression was slightly lower in the PGel hydrogel group than in the control group, the difference was not statistically significant. These findings underscore the significant influence that the bioactive constituents of Chlorella extract have on the modulation of immune responses within wounds. The application of CPGel hydrogels appears to catalyze a pivotal phenotypic transition from the proinflammatory M1 macrophage state to the anti-inflammatory M2 state within the wound environment. This shift effectively curbs the release of proinflammatory cytokines, thereby fostering a more conducive environment for the acceleration of the wound healing process.

In this study, we successfully engineered a multifunctional hydrogel (CPGel) through solvent extraction of Chlorella and green self-assembly with gelatin and PEG, synergizing natural bioactive compounds with biomaterial innovation. CPGel exemplifies a 3R therapeutic strategy for diabetic wound healing: Remove: Complete eradication of bacterial pathogens (E. coli and S. aureus) via dual mechanisms-PEG-induced osmotic stress and Chlorella-derived antimicrobial compound-achieving 100 % antibacterial efficacy. Remodel: Dynamic microenvironment modulation through 65 % ROS scavenging to mitigate oxidative stress and immunomodulation via M1-to-M2 macrophage polarization, resolving chronic inflammation and restoring immune balance. Repair: Accelerated tissue regeneration driven by 9-fold angiogenesis (α-SMA expression) and 2-fold collagen I deposition, enabling robust extracellular matrix remodelling and full-thickness wound closure within 21 days in diabetic mice. Mechanically superior to conventional gelatin hydrogels (8 × compressive strength: 4.16 MPa; 33 × tensile strength: 627 kPa), CPGel combines antifreezing resilience (−100 °C), transparency, and injectable adhesion, ensuring clinical adaptability. By harmonizing traditional Chinese medicine principles with toxin-free, scalable fabrication, CPGel addresses critical challenges in chronic wound care. Future efforts will prioritize large-scale production and clinical validation, leveraging the 3R framework to advance next-generation therapies rooted in sustainable, nature-inspired design. This work underscores the transformative potential of integrating herbal bioactives with engineered biomaterials for unmet medical needs.

title: Functional Hydrogels for Treatment of Chronic Wounds
abstract: Chronic wounds severely affect 1–2% of the population in developed countries. It has been reported that nearly 6.5 million people in the United States suffer from at least one chronic wound in their lifetime. The treatment of chronic wounds is critical for maintaining the physical and mental well-being of patients and improving their quality of life. There are a host of methods for the treatment of chronic wounds, including debridement, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, ultrasound, and electromagnetic therapies, negative pressure wound therapy, skin grafts, and hydrogel dressings. Among these, hydrogel dressings represent a promising and viable choice because their tunable functional properties, such as biodegradability, adhesivity, and antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and pre-angiogenic bioactivities, can accelerate the healing of chronic wounds. This review summarizes the types of chronic wounds, phases of the healing process, and key therapeutic approaches. Hydrogel-based dressings are reviewed for their multifunctional properties and their advantages for the treatment of chronic wounds. Examples of commercially available hydrogel dressings are also provided to demonstrate their effectiveness over other types of wound dressings for chronic wound healing.

sections.text: Skin is the largest organ in the human body, and it provides a vital barrier against the outside environment. Severe cutaneous wounds or burns trigger the healing process in a well-synchronized sequence of controlled stages: hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and re-modeling [1,2]. In a normal wound healing process, these stages proceed in a specific order with each stage having a proper duration. The duration of the healing stages varies for different wound types [2,3]. In the next subsection, wound healing phases are described.

Wound healing is a natural process comprised of a series of distinct events that make up four highly regulated phases: homeostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and re-modeling (Figure 1). For a wound to heal properly, the stages should take place in the correct order and within a certain time frame. In adults, the wound healing process involves homeostasis, an inflammatory response, differentiation, multiplication, movement of mesenchymal cells, angiogenesis, brief re-epithelialization, and the synthesis, crosslinking and arrangement of collagen to give solidarity to the recuperating tissue [1,2]. Homeostasis is the initial step of wound healing. It serves as the body’s first response to damage. Blood arteries in the trauma region contract to reduce blood loss instantly. Platelets are then released along with fibrin to create a thrombus or blood clot to seal the damaged blood arteries and prevent blood loss [3]. Inflammation occurs immediately after homeostasis. The vasodilation of local capillaries helps with the transfer of leukocytes and exudates near the wound site to prevent infection throughout the wound healing process. In addition, pro-inflammatory cytokines and growth factors, including transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), fibroblast growth factor (FGF), and epidermal growth factor (EGF), are released in the surrounding wound tissue. Meanwhile, neutrophils clear cellular debris from the wound area and kill invading microorganisms by generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) and releasing toxic proteases. Macrophages are critical to facilitate the regeneration of the skin tissue [3,4,5]. Macrophages produce cytokines in the initial stages to enhance the immune response by attracting and stimulating additional leukocytes. Moreover, macrophages induce apoptosis and clear apoptotic cells, including neutrophils. Redness and discomfort around the wound bed are commonly observed at this stage. Proliferation is the third phase of wound healing. In this phase, granulated tissue with an extracellular matrix (ECM) composed of new connective tissue and blood vessels is formed in the presence of an appropriate amount of moisture and oxygen. The movement of T-lymphocytes (T-cells) into a wound bed plays an important role in granulated tissue formation. These T-cells secrete biomolecules, such as fibroblast growth factor 7 (FGF-7), keratinocyte growth factors (KGFs), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), to regulate fibroblast and keratinocyte expansion during this stage [6]. Re-modeling is the fourth and final phase of wound healing. In this stage, the ECM of the wounded tissue is reconstituted to be similar to healthy tissue. This phase is mostly regulated by differentiated myofibroblasts. Collagen, the main ECM component, is synthesized and accumulates in the granulation tissue to restore the tensile strength and elasticity that is found in normal skin tissue [7]. During this stage, many of the newly produced capillaries regress, and the vascular density of the wound is restored [3,8]. Overall, various cell types and biomolecules participate in the different wound healing phases, and their activity plays a crucial role in wound repair. The most efficient treatment approach might be chosen based on the healing stage of a specific wound. The different types of wounds are classified in the next section.

Skin wounds are classified based on the duration of the healing stages. If each stage of the wound healing process proceeds in a timely and organized manner, wounds will completely heal, both anatomically and functionally, within three months after the initial injury. These types of wounds are called non-chronic wounds. A delay in any of the healing stages, however, causes wounds to become chronic. This may result in a prolonged healing time or a non-healing wound, which might cause skin to lose some of its anatomical or functional properties. Delays in the wound healing processes typically occur during the inflammatory phase. The most common types of chronic wounds are diabetic ulcers, pressure ulcers, and vascular ulcers (Table 1) [9]. The effects of the chronic wound type on the healing process are discussed in the next section.

Diabetic ulcers usually develop in patients with peripheral neuropathy [16]. Thus, the patients are unable to notice recurrent mild damage on their legs or feet. With this condition, an increase in glucose levels leads to a rise in the level of ROS, nitric oxide blockade, DNA alteration, protein kinase C elevation, ischemia, and inflammation around the wound. The severity can vary between patients, which may change the length of time required for wound healing. The variation in wound healing times is caused by variations in growth factor synthesis, angiogenesis, cell migration and proliferation, collagen deposition, and ECM modification by proteases [3]. Pressure ulcers are another type of chronic wound. Pressure ulcers are most seen in individuals with limited movement and neuropathies. A physical stress induced by prolonged direct pressure and shear forces on the skin can cause injury-related hypoxia and ischemia. In response, adipocytes trigger an inflammatory response. Therefore, higher concentrations of neutrophils are generally seen in patients with pressure ulcers. Necrotic tissue is also observed in these patients due to increased levels of interstitial fluid. This type of chronic wound may become more severe in patients with vascular insufficiencies [3]. There are two types of vascular ulcers: arterial insufficiency (ischemic) ulcers and blood vessel (venous) ulcers. Ischemic ulcers arise from atherosclerosis, in which prohibited perfusion flow results in ischemia and tissue necrosis. Venous ulcers are characterized by venous insufficiencies. Hence, these ulcers are frequently accompanied by edema, varicose veins, and hyper-pigmented zones. In addition, the accumulation of hemosiderin, an iron storage complex and the breakdown product of heme, is seen, which may lead to stiffness in the legs. Venous ulcers may be preceded by sensations of stiffness and discomfort in the legs and limbs similar to arterial insufficiency ulcers [3]. The stages of the wound healing process for different types of chronic wounds need to be studied to understand the mechanisms and to develop proper treatment methodologies. The next section focuses on possible treatment approaches for chronic wounds (Table 2).

Debridement is a well-structured, initial clinical approach to remove non-viable tissue in the wound bed for any type of wound [17]. Debridement can be performed by surgery, conventional dressing, larvae, enzyme preparation, polysaccharide beads, or hydrogels [18]. All methods show similar activity, and the debridement process must be performed by clinical specialists. If the amount of removed non-viable tissue is not sufficient, the residual non-viable tissue may cause damage to the surrounding tissues. Therefore, the debridement process may need to be repeated. However, removal of too much non-viable tissue can lead to the loss of some viable tissue and lengthen the healing time [25,26]. A single debridement process with the loss of a small number of viable cells is optimal for preserving the viability of the wound area, which helps with the reconstitution of skin tissue. In addition, patients might experience pain during and after the debridement process. The effectiveness of debridement differs from one patient to another. The overall debridement process can be a costly treatment approach [19].

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is based on the use of a special oxygen chamber which exposes the patient to high pressured oxygen to increase the oxygen concentration of blood in the wound area [27]. This method is mostly preferred for diabetic ulcers [20,27]. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy has been shown to improve and shorten the wound healing process in cases where revascularization of the damaged tissue failed or was not feasible. The administration of hyperbaric oxygen therapy, however, requires costly specialized hardware. In addition, it is usually limited to diabetic wounds and pressure ulcers.

Ultrasound therapy uses sound waves to relieve pain by warming up the wound area. Side effects of ultrasound therapy include damage or burns in the endothelial tissues. These effects often occur when process parameters are not optimized according to the specific needs of a patient. Another wound treatment approach is electromagnetic therapy. This method is based on the application of weak electromagnetic waves with frequencies ranging from 30 to 70 GHz and power densities up to 10 mWcm−2 to relieve pain in the wound area [21]. The use of this method has been suggested for the treatment of venous and pressure ulcers and surgical incisions. Neither ultrasound nor electromagnetic therapies have been clinically proven to significantly influence the wound healing process [21,22].

Negative pressure wound therapy is also known as vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) therapy [23]. In this method, an airtight dressing, which removes air and fluid from the wound via a small tube connected to a pump, is used to cover the wound. The negative pressure can also help increase blood flow around the wound. This approach increases moisture and oxygen levels around the wound area and therefore enhances the healing process in large chronic wounds. It can be used in both primary and secondary treatment methods. VAC therapy is typically used in fully equipped healthcare facilities. The treatment procedure not only limits the mobility of the patient, but may also cause discomfort due to noise.

Skin grafts are generally transplanted to wound sites that may not close on their own. In this method, donor skin tissue is taken from another part of the patient’s body, or a graft is produced from a human donor or synthetically [24]. This approach, however, requires the expertise of medical professionals at fully equipped health institutions. Moreover, skin grafting operations are typically not cost-effective.

Wound dressings are used to cover wounds to provide optimum conditions for the wound healing process [28,29,30,31].
